SpaceX has won approval from US communications regulators for its Starmind constellation. Up to 1 million satellites would process AI data in orbit.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million satellites for orbital data centers, according to Reuters. The Starmind constellation of orbital compute modules is intended to meet part of the rapidly growing demand for AI computing power on Earth. The agency also approved radio links that let SpaceX monitor and control the satellites if their optical connections fail.

science-mind-7a47b5d7af.headline: Has AI just cracked Internet encryption? Rumoured ‘bombshell’ stuns scientists
science-mind-7a47b5d7af.fulltext:
Artificial-intelligence agents have already begun to wreak havoc by hacking into servers around the world, either spontaneously or directed by humans. Now, a threat is emerging that is on a whole other scale.
Several computer scientists have suggested on social media that the leading AI laboratories — companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic, both in San Francisco, California — have discovered algorithms that could derail the security of Internet communications.
‘If we can solve Riemann, what can’t we do?’: mathematicians shocked and excited by AI breakthroughs
“I’m virtually certain, from multiple reliable sources, that the AI labs are now sitting on one or more bombshells,” computer scientist Scott Aaronson wrote yesterday on his blog. The details are still hazy, added Aaronson, who is at the University of Texas at Austin. “Until I either see details or hear directly from someone at a lab, I feel much, much less confident about the specific nature of those bombshells.”
The algorithms are rumoured to target the information-scrambling system known as RSA, which relies on the mathematics of prime numbers, as well as more-advanced technologies.
While the rumours could not be confirmed, other breakthroughs announced by the AI companies this week make researchers cautiously optimistic that the mathematics of encryption could eventually come to help.
Nature examines the threat, and what can be done about it.
What are the rumours?
Several researchers say they have heard that some of the leading AI laboratories have discovered algorithms capable of breaking public-key cryptography in ‘polynomial time’ (or ‘P’ in computer-science shorthand).
Public-key cryptography helps to secure everything from banking apps to Internet browsers. It relies on mathematical problems that are considered practically impossible for computers to solve within a reasonable amount of time.
An algorithm that could solve these problems in polynomial time would change that. It means the time needed to solve a problem would increase relatively slowly as the problem gets larger. For example, a password of length n could be broken in a number of steps proportional to the square or cube of its size (n² or n³).
The race to save the Internet from quantum hackers
Theoretical computer scientists tend to think of P problems as relatively easy to solve, especially compared with problems that require exponential time, where the number of steps might grow as 2n, for example. As n gets larger — or a password gets longer — the time required by an exponential algorithm quickly exceeds that of any polynomial one.
In practical terms, an algorithm that could break public-key cryptography in polynomial time could undermine much of the security on which the Internet relies.
Would these algorithms immediately threaten the whole Internet?
It depends on which encryption systems they could crack, and how efficiently they could do so.
One of the most ubiquitous techniques for establishing public keys is to multiply two large prime numbers. This technique, called RSA, was long believed to be secure because ‘cracking the code’ requires factoring that product back into the original primes, a much slower process (at least, without a powerful quantum computer, which does not yet exist). One of the rumours now circulating is that the AI labs have found an algorithm that can do this.
But even though a polynomial-time algorithm could be very powerful on paper, it could still be impossible to use except for the shortest passwords. An algorithm requiring n10000steps, for example, be very impractical to apply.
However, proving that a problem is in ‘P’, even if the polynomial-time solution is practically useless, has usually been followed by improvements that have eventually led to efficient solutions. “The issue is that the idea that [the problem] was hard — because of needing exponential time — is dead,” Aaronson tells Nature.
So is all public-key cryptography doomed?
Not necessarily. This type of worst-case scenario hinges on a long-standing open question known as ‘P = NP’: could every problem whose solution can be checked in polynomial time also be solved in polynomial time? If so, problems that underpin essentially all public-key cryptography could become much easier to crack.
Quantum-computing pioneer warns of complacency over Internet security
But most researchers think that this is unlikely. In fact, some recent AI-aided results have made them cautiously optimistic. Earlier this week, both Anthropic and OpenAI announced results in theoretical computer science that suggest that many similar problems could be hard to solve. Before the recent explosion in AI-aided maths, each of those advances would have been hailed as the computer-science breakthrough of the decade, Aaronson says.
Ryan Williams, a computer scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge, agrees. “I am definitely blown away by the latest developments.” One especially interesting result, he says, shows that for a ubiquitous type of computation called matrix multiplication, the exponent in a polynomial-time algorithm cannot be too small. “Underneath the hood, it seems to provide a brand-new framework for proving limitations on efficient computation,” says Williams.

world-b661f1d123.headline: What would happen if Russia detonated a nuclear weapon in space?
world-b661f1d123.fulltext:
German media outlets have reported, citing western intelligence agency assessments, that such a satellite could be launched within 60 days and would be operational shortly afterwards.
Here we look at the implications of a nuclear weapon being detonated in space.
What is the report saying?
A report by the German broadcasters NDR and WDR and the newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung said western intelligence services, including Germany’s Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND) intelligence service and armed forces, had exchanged information showing that a nuclear-enabled satellite, named Sputnik-S, was assembled several years ago and is stationed in the Moscow region. It could be launched this year. A German government spokesperson said it was taking the intelligence reports “very seriously”.
What impact could a nuclear device have if exploded in orbit?
In space, where there is no atmosphere, there is no mushroom cloud. Instead, the energy from a nuclear explosion is released as radiation. A detonation would be particularly damaging in low Earth orbit, or up to 1,200 miles above Earth, where most satellites operate.
Jonathan McDowell, an astrophysicist and honorary professor at the Durham University Space Research Centre in the UK, said the main effects were twofold: everything within line of sight of the detonation could be zapped by X-rays and other forms of radiation which could knock out or damage satellites within thousands of miles; secondly, radiation particles could be emitted into the lower atmosphere and form a new “Van Allen belt”, the term for two belts of radiation that circle the Earth and shield it from the impact of solar storms.
It would be a replay of an event in 1962 when the US detonated a thermonuclear bomb 250 miles above Earth’s surface – in low Earth orbit – in an event called Starfish Prime. There were many fewer satellites then but it shortened the life of two craft: the Telstar 1 and Ariel-1 satellites.
“Starfish caused severe radiation over a period of months to at least half the satellites then working on orbit, which was not very many at that point,” said McDowell.
Keith Ryden, a professor of space engineering at the University of Surrey in the UK, said low Earth orbit satellites were vulnerable to bursts of radiation.
“Since natural levels of radiation are relatively low in this region, satellites located there are not designed for high radiation levels so they would be vulnerable to unexpected increases,” he says.
What is the most damaging area of orbit for this to happen in?
There are about 17,000 satellites in lower Earth orbit, including satellites important to weather forecasting, climate monitoring and the military as well as Elon Musk’s network of satellites that form the Starlink broadband network. The latter is crucial to assisting Ukraine’s efforts in repelling the invasion of Russia.
The International Space Station, in which Russia is a partner, is also in low Earth orbit. Musk’s proposed constellation of space datacentres would operate there as well.
Satellites handling TV broadcast, GPS and other communications are in higher orbits that are less easy for a nuclear weapon to affect.
How long would it take to recover activity in the affected area of orbit?
McDowell said the artificial Van Allen belt caused by Starfish Prime was around for five years.
“There will be immediate impacts from a detonation but there are lasting environmental effects that will damage satellites in the longer run. It could take several years, up to a decade, for the trapped particles to diffuse out of the radiation belt,” he said.
Ryden added: “Just as important, the space industry would not have the capacity to rebuild and launch the required number of spacecraft in a short time.”
Would activity on Earth be immediately affected by an explosion?
Hundreds of miles below the Starfish Prime explosion, streetlights in Hawaii were knocked out, burglar alarms were set off in the area, and phone calls were disrupted.
“There might be an impact on computers and electronic systems in the region of earth where the explosion is visible,” said McDowell.
Ryden added that Starfish and other nuclear tests took place over sparsely populated areas so the location of the detonation was key.
“It does depend a lot on where the detonation happens,” he said.
Starfish Prime also created stunning aurora effects as the sky was lit up in shades of green, yellow, red and, according to one report, “tremendous white rainbows”.
“There would be huge auroral effects. It would not be a subtle thing. It’s hard to be subtle with nukes,” said McDowell.
Is Russia likely to detonate a nuclear warhead in space?
A European security official told the Guardian that they were doubtful that Russia would detonate a nuclear device in space. They said it could cause significant damage to western economies, but that it stood to significantly harm Russia as well. Such an explosion would be hard to control and would probably damage Russia’s own satellites, as well as, potentially, China’s. “It would be shooting themselves in the leg,” they said.
They pointed at Russia’s nuclear blackmail earlier in its war in Ukraine, including when Russia put its nuclear forces on high alert in 2022, followed by movements of troops and weapons. “They were bluffing then – and this looks like a bluff now,” said the official. McDowell said he was sceptical about Russia detonating a nuclear weapon in space, because it was “such a stupid idea” to commit what would be viewed as an act of war.

world-276364b19c.headline: Trump calls GDP figures ‘fake’, demands probe of his own Commerce Department
world-276364b19c.fulltext:
Search the way you think. Try our AI-powered search to find news faster.
US President Donald Trump on Thursday accused his Commerce Department of purposely issuing incorrect economic growth figures before the midterm elections and said he wants to launch an investigation.
Trump has repeatedly sought to undermine trust in economic data that fails to match his claims of a historic boom, a pattern that threatens the credibility of figures needed by businesses, financial markets and consumers when making investments.
His latest complaint concerns data issued by the Commerce Department on Wednesday that revised gross domestic product in the third quarter to 4.3 per cent on an annual basis, up from a prior estimate of 3.4 per cent.
The department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis routinely updates its economic data to improve its accuracy. GDP figures, monthly jobs reports and other data are regularly revised. Those updates occur on a pre-scheduled basis without regard to the political calendar.
But the president claimed on social media that it was a “massive, and purposeful, error” and linked it to the poor performance for Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections that gave Democrats control of both houses of Congress.
“It was just revealed that the REAL Numbers on the Economy, published before the Election, were FAKE, and a correction was issued yesterday by the people in the Government Agency that does these numbers,” Trump posted.
“Why wasn’t the correct number issued before the Election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation.”
The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The government is largely closed on Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday.
This is the latest instance of Trump questioning the integrity of economic data he feels is unfavourable to him without providing evidence that revisions are politically motivated.
In August 2025, Trump fired the head of the Bureau of Labour Statistics after a decidedly weak jobs report. That report said only 73,000 jobs were added in July 2025 and showed that 258,000 fewer jobs were added in May and June than previously reported.
Trump has claimed that he deserves credit for powering stronger economic growth, but voters do not share the president’s belief that the economy is strong.
In the midterms, 76 per cent described economic conditions as “not so good” or “poor”, according to the AP Voter Poll, an extensive survey of the electorate. About two-thirds of voters said Trump’s own policies had fuelled inflation.
The president in his social media post ignored that the same federal agency on Wednesday also reported that a key measure of inflation – the personal consumption expenditures price index – accelerated to an annual pace of 3.8 per cent in October.

india-593d00a188.headline: US links India export edge to cheap Chinese manufacturing inputs
india-593d00a188.fulltext:
US links India export edge to cheap Chinese manufacturing inputs
The USTR alleges India's reliance on Chinese intermediate goods and industrial policies gives its exporters an artificial cost advantage, harming US producers.
 premium 
5 min read  Last Updated : Nov 26 2026 | 11:21 PM IST
Listen to This Article
The United States Trade Representative (USTR) alleged that India’s growing reliance on Chinese manufacturing inputs, coupled with its own industrial policies, gave Indian exporters an artificial cost advantage and created “economic security risks” for Washington. 
In its November 25 report on India’s manufacturing policies under Section 301 of the US Trade Act, the USTR said India’s trade imbalances were partly due to its reliance on “cheap Chinese inputs” while exporting large volumes of finished goods to the US, particularly pharmaceuticals and medical devices, steel, solar products, and information and communication technology products. 
“India has failed to restrict imports of these goods in sectors in which China exhibits structural excess capacity and production. These data reveal that US products compete with Chinese inputs in India, and Indian manufacturers’ increasing reliance on non-market economy (NME) inputs results in lost opportunities for US firms to manufacture or expand capacity for upstream goods as well,” it said.  
Citing Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development data, the report said that 3.8 per cent of value added in India’s exports to US in 2022 was attributable to China. In the same year, China’s share of value added in US exports was 1.6 per cent.
“ADB data similarly indicate that the value-added of Chinese inputs into India’s manufacturing exports to the US has hovered between 2.3 per cent in 2017, increasing to 4.4 per cent in 2024. Structural excess capacity and production in India suppress prices, investment, and production in the US in sectors that are critical to the functioning of the US economy,” it added. 
Brahma Chellaney, professor of strategic studies at the Centre for Policy Research, said in a post on X that the USTR’s Section 301 determination against India symbolised a significant shift in US trade doctrine.
“Rather than targeting specific instances of dumping or intellectual property theft, Washington is effectively treating India's developmental industrial policy itself as an offence by labelling its ‘industrial plans to expand manufacturing’ as ‘unreasonable acts’. With millions of Indians entering the workforce annually, expanding manufacturing, which accounts for 15–17 per cent of gross domestic product, is a fundamental developmental necessity to mitigate an unemployment crisis and make the economy more competitive,” he added.
India’s commerce department has rejected the US claim of structural ‘excess capacity’ in any sector, emphasising that trade-related concerns should be addressed within the framework of trade deal negotiations between the two countries.
The US administration on Wednesday proposed imposing tariffs of up to 25 per cent on Indian goods, citing structural excess capacity, but offered to lower the rate to 17 per cent if New Delhi and Washington concluded a trade deal.
The USTR said surging imports of Chinese inputs distorted competitive conditions in the Indian market and enhanced the artificial competitiveness of Indian downstream products manufactured using those inputs.
The report said India had become increasingly reliant on China for imports of intermediate consumption goods.
“India’s value of intermediate consumption imports from China is up $44 billion, or 97 per cent, between 2017 and 2025; by comparison, the value of intermediate consumption imports into the US from China is down $30 billion, or -21 per cent, over the same period. India and the US both had a 14 per cent share of intermediate consumption imports from China in 2017. However, for India, the share of imports from China increased to 16 per cent in 2025, while for the US, this share dropped to 7 per cent,” it said.
The report said India’s failure to effectively monitor and address imports and foreign direct investment (FDI) from NMEs such as China harmed US producers and exporters.
“Failures by India to address FDI aimed at increasing manufacturing for purposes of producing excess capacity from China also permit China to export its excess capacity through Indian industries. The result is distorted competitive conditions for US firms, and distorted prices, lost sales or exports, and diminished revenues in India and global markets,” it said.
Citing India’s Make in India, Self-Reliant India (Atmanirbhar Bharat), and production-linked incentive policies, the report said India had pursued a growth strategy through the development and implementation of industrial plans that had led to non-market-driven capacity expansion, production and exports in key manufacturing sectors.
“Following on decades of industrial plans, in recent years India has engaged in more aggressive industrial policy to increase the size of its manufacturing sector and boost key sectors,” it said.
The report observed that India’s goods trade surplus with the US had risen from $42.5 billion in 2023 to $57.3 billion in 2025, even as the country ran an overall global goods trade deficit of around $309 billion last year.
Chellaney said that while the US deployed hundreds of billions of dollars in massive, state-backed industrial subsidies, including under the CHIPS and Science Act and the Inflation Reduction Act, it was penalising India for offering comparatively modest industrial incentives.
“The report constitutes yet another coercive negotiating lever to extract further Indian concessions…In this light, signing the US-India bilateral trade agreement with an unpredictable Trump administration that keeps shifting the goalposts would be almost a fool’s errand for India,” he said.

ai-ab8e8d3251.fulltext:

India launches indigenous Chariot-1 Foundation Models to strengthen sovereign AI capabilities
                    The Union Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has launched Chariot-1 Foundation Models to boost AI capabilities. This initiative is part of the IndiaAI Mission aimed at developing indigenous technology. The Chariot-1 model suite includes an 11-billion-parameter Large Language Model and a multilingual Text-to-Speech model. These models are designed to improve efficiency and speech generation across various Indian languages.
                                    
In a push to strengthen India's sovereign artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities, the Union Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) Secretary S Krishnan launched the indigenously developed Chariot-1 Foundation Models under the IndiaAI Mission, according to a statement by MeitY.
According to the release, Chariot Artificial Intelligence Pvt. Ltd. is among the first four teams selected under the IndiaAI Mission to develop sovereign foundation models.
The Chariot-1 model suite comprises a Large Language Model (LLM) and a Text-to-Speech (TTS) model, both pre-trained from scratch in India.
The Chariot-1 LLM is an 11-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model, with four billion active parameters per token. It is available in three variants of 10.7 billion, 1.7 billion and 745 million parameters, catering to different computational requirements and deployment environments.
Meanwhile, the Chariot-1 TTS model is capable of generating speech in English and 10 Indian languages, including Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Gujarati, Punjabi and Odia, according to the release.
One of the key features of the speech model is its ability to understand context and determine how numbers, dates, currencies, units, URLs and abbreviations should be pronounced.
According to the ministry, this capability enables more natural and context-aware speech generation, addressing a key challenge in developing speech technologies for real-world applications.
The speech model recorded over 97 per cent verbalisation accuracy on the Async TTS Pronunciation Benchmark, which comprises 1,029 real-world sentences and 2,251 instances of non-standard text across 42 categories, the Ministry said.
It also recorded a character error rate of 7.60 per cent in Hindi and an average character error rate of 6.47 per cent across nine other Indian languages, the lowest among the systems evaluated in the reported tests.
"By supporting teams developing sovereign foundation models, the IndiaAI Mission is enabling researchers, innovators and enterprises to pursue ambitious AI research and translate it into homegrown technological solutions," the release said.

beyond-your-beat-6c7c9a9ab2.headline: Death-sentenced Sheikh Hasina's planned return puts Bangladesh on edge - and India in a bind
beyond-your-beat-6c7c9a9ab2.fulltext:
Death-sentenced Sheikh Hasina's planned return puts Bangladesh on edge - and India in a bind
Sheikh Hasina has repeatedly vowed to return to Bangladesh.
Now the ousted prime minister has put a date on her homecoming - 16 December - and even outlined how she intends to make the journey.
The government in Dhaka, which had previously dismissed the prospect, is taking her latest declaration more seriously.
Hasina, 79, who fled to Delhi in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her 15-year rule, plans to go back on Victory Day, the anniversary of Bangladesh's triumph over Pakistan in the 1971 liberation war, her spokesperson said.
She was sentenced to death after being convicted of crimes against humanity for her role in the crackdown, in a trial held in her absence that raised questions about due process. Her Awami League party is banned in Bangladesh. The UN says as many as 1,400 people were killed by security forces during the uprising.
The government says she would be arrested immediately if she returned and has promised to carry out the death sentence.
Hasina now wants the Bangladesh government to arrange a flight from Delhi. If that fails, she could travel commercially or cross the land border.
"She is even prepared to walk into Bangladesh," Abu Obaidha Arin, a key aide to Hasina, told the BBC.
India and Bangladesh share a 4,096km (2,545 mile) border across five Indian states - West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Her supporters, Arin said, had identified nine possible crossing points. "This is a carefully thought-out, precise plan. This is serious."
Dhaka has responded with defiance, insisting Hasina must be extradited.
"Reality and desire are different things," Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs, told reporters in Dhaka. "[The reality is] she's not a regular commercial passenger. She can only be brought back in handcuffs."
India's foreign ministry said on Wednesday that Hasina's extradition request was being examined through the "established process", adding that a voluntary return would be a separate matter.
Many in Dhaka believe Hasina's declaration is more than a promise of homecoming.
They believe it is an attempt to test the government's authority, force her way back into the political conversation and exploit divisions among the parties that united to oust her. It also threatens to turn India's unresolved problem of sheltering a former ally into a more immediate diplomatic crisis.
The date is significant. Hasina is invoking Victory Day to reclaim her place in Bangladesh's founding narrative. Aides say she has spent months trying to keep her party alive in exile.
Arin says Hasina has been in regular contact with party leaders and workers through interactive audio conversations on Telegram, keeping alive a network that might otherwise have been difficult to sustain from exile.
Over the past 18 months, he says, she has held more than 300 such meetings, reaching supporters across all 64 districts and the country's 300 constituencies. They are organised through the Awami League's 78 units and "can last four or five hours".
The meetings allow Hasina to listen directly to party workers, hear their grievances and understand what is happening on the ground, Arin says. He insists the response has been substantial and claims the party "could mobilise five million people to welcome her along the route from the border to Dhaka, forming a human chain".
"We have the organisational capacity to make that happen," he says.
That may be an ambitious claim. The Awami League remains a mass party with millions of supporters, but it is banned and largely shut out of mainstream politics. Much of its leadership is abroad, in jail or underground. Police have arrested supporters and filed thousands of cases against party workers.
Yet its supporters have continued to take to the streets, staging flash protests that have grown more frequent and confrontational in recent months.
Several districts have reported bomb attacks, arson and vandalism, though responsibility for some incidents remains disputed.
Gopalganj, Hasina's ancestral district, has proved particularly difficult for the authorities to control.
Awami League supporters have attacked police stations, torched vehicles and targeted homes and offices belonging to ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) leaders, reports say. Highways have been blocked with felled trees and burning tyres, bringing traffic to a standstill. In some areas, police have withdrawn amid fears of further attacks.
Supporters have staged 40 demonstrations and more than 140 riots up to 23 November, according to data from conflict monitoring group Acled (Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project). At least 11 people, including two civilians, have been killed in political violence this month, six directly linked to the unrest, the group says.
The party's ability to cause disruption, however, is not necessarily evidence of a broad resurgence.
Many in Dhaka remain sceptical that Hasina will actually return, viewing the announcement as a means of galvanising a demoralised party.
Yet the Awami League has achieved something politically: it is back in the conversation. Immediately after Hasina's fall, even mentioning the party was taboo. Now its future is being debated across the political spectrum.
Shafiqul Alam, editor of the English-language daily Daily Waadaa and former press secretary to the Muhammad Yunus-led interim government, believes the party is "exploiting cracks in the unity forged during the uprising".
He told the BBC that "disagreements" over the July Charter, proposed constitutional changes and the referendum have "widened divisions" between the elected BNP government and rivals Jamaat-e-Islami and the youth-led National Citizen Party (NCP).
"The Awami League sees an opening," Alam told the BBC. "The party believes this is an opportune moment to take to the streets, exploiting a weakened police force and divisions among the forces of the July uprising."
Analysts say if Hasina returns it could just as easily deepen hostility as revive her party's fortunes. The government has framed the sporadic recent violence as terrorism, while supporters insist their demonstrations are peaceful and accuse the authorities of repression.
The larger question is whether Bangladesh can sustain the exclusion of a political constituency as substantial as the Awami League without creating another source of instability.
For India, the dilemma is increasingly difficult to manage.
Delhi has sheltered Hasina, but her public remarks have angered Dhaka, which wants her extradited. India has sought to repair ties through diplomatic outreach and talks on trade, border security and other bilateral issues, but relations remain strained.
The chill is striking: nearly 10 months into his tenure, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has yet to visit India.
A trip was reportedly in the offing in August, but Hasina's press conference in Delhi proved a setback to efforts to reset relations.
Avinash Paliwal, who teaches politics and international studies at SOAS University of London, argues that Hasina's latest announcement has "shifted the burden of choice to Dhaka rather than Delhi".
Delhi, he says, "feels it has tried its best" to work with Rahman's government over the past 10 months - "from appointing a political heavyweight as high commissioner with cabinet rank to offering fresh talks on security and trade".
"The failure of this outreach has left India disillusioned with Dhaka. India seems to have decided that bilateral relations will likely remain tense whatever it does, so there is little reason to stop Hasina from stirring the political pot."
Delhi has the leverage to restrain Hasina from making political statements on Indian soil, Paliwal argues, but may not want to exercise it.
Nor, in his view, is it in India's interest to see the Awami League permanently excluded from Bangladeshi politics.
"The political party still enjoys pockets of support across Bangladesh and is weaved into the social and political fabric of the country," he says. "So, yes, it is in India's interest, and also in Bangladesh's long-term interests, to rehabilitate the Awami League and take the path of political reconciliation."
That view is increasingly contested in Dhaka.
"There is a perception in Bangladesh that India wants to rehabilitate the Awami League. There are issues India has not resolved, including the extradition of Hasina. India has also not renewed the transit facilities that could benefit Bangladeshi garment exporters, while the Ganges water treaty is nearing expiry without much progress. But has India done enough to win back trust?" says Alam.
"For now, only tourist and medical visas have resumed. Everything else remains in limbo."
A Dhaka-based foreign-policy expert, who asked not to be named, says the two countries remain locked in "mutual frustration".
Hasina, he says, remains central to the impasse. "She remains the elephant in the room, but we also have to find a way to move beyond Hasina."
Paliwal argues that the least damaging outcome for India would be Hasina returning to face a fresh trial, with the Awami League rehabilitated under a different operational leadership.
"It will reintroduce a degree of balance in Bangladeshi politics, and will afford India space to protect its long-term interests and equities better," he says.
For now, 16 December is not yet a confirmed journey. But Hasina has already succeeded in making her return a question that neither Dhaka nor Delhi can ignore.
"December could be chaotic. Everyone in Dhaka is on edge," says the foreign-policy expert, warning of protests and confrontation as Hasina's proposed return date approaches - and the possibility that it could be postponed yet again.
"Hasina is unlikely to return, as she would face a death sentence. But her comments have clearly galvanized her supporters," says Pearl Pandya, Acled's South Asia analyst.
But the impasse is also complicating India's ties with Bangladesh. As Paliwal puts it, the "next window of serious negotiations will now open only after Hasina returns to Dhaka, or Dhaka relents under pressure and returns to the table".

Supreme Court tightens food warning labels in new setback for industry
India is in the midst of an unprecedented food safety crackdown, including nationwide raids against restaurants, amid concern over poor hygiene and standards. The government's plan for front-of-pack red warning labels came after heated public debate on the lack of such measures.
On Thursday, the Supreme Court said the government needs to tighten its proposal, mandating separate hexagon-shaped warning label for high salt, sugar and fat on the front of packs, not only one as proposed earlier by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India.
The authority shall ensure that a separate hexagon for each "nutrient of concern, each containing the word high fat, high sugar, high salt... rather than a single combined hexagon," the Supreme Court said while pronouncing the verdict.
The order will be a setback to the $100 billion food and drinks industry that has long opposed such labels, but was welcome by health activists who have called for them.
"This is certainly a landmark development in the nutritional history of the country," said Rajiv ‌Shankar Dvivedi, the lead counsel for non-profit "3S And Our Health" which had challenged the government in the Supreme Court for the lack of warning labels.

ai-2cb2c6a452.headline: Lowdown: How Australia’s new online safety law will change social media, AI chatbots and app stores
ai-2cb2c6a452.fulltext:
Australia’s Parliament passed a law on November 25 that makes tech companies responsible for preventing harm to users before it happens. The Digital Duty of Care Act covers social media, messaging apps, games, search engines, app stores, AI chatbots and even internet equipment makers.
Companies that fail to protect users face fines of up to 5% of their global turnover. Users who suffer harm can also sue platforms directly, on their own or as a group. Platforms that lose must pay the users’ legal costs.
What you need to know:
- What it does: Platforms must identify the risks their services create and reduce them. They can’t cite cost as a reason not to act.
- Children: Social media platforms can’t show under-16s recommendations based on their account data or features such as endless feeds, like counts and stories.
- Penalties: Companies face fines of up to 5% of global turnover or A$109.2 million, whichever is higher.
- Lawsuits: Individuals and groups can sue, and the costs rules favour them.
- Timing: The main duty applies 12 months after royal assent. New powers against fake nude apps and faster takedowns start the next day.
Why did Australia pass this law?
Australia’s online safety rules have mostly worked after the fact. A user reports harmful content, and the eSafety Commissioner, the country’s online safety regulator, orders the platform to remove it. Industry groups wrote codes of conduct to cover the rest.
The new law asks platforms to fix risks at the design stage instead. “This is about kids being radicalised on the school bus on their way home,” Communications Minister Anika Wells told reporters at a press conference.
It builds on Australia’s social media age restrictions, which have barred under-16s from holding accounts on major platforms since December 10, 2025. Wells said the new law will follow the same path, with “a 12-month transition, like the social media minimum age did.”
What is a “digital duty of care”?
A duty of care is a legal obligation to take reasonable steps to prevent foreseeable harm to others. The law applies it to online services. Anyone running one must “take appropriate action to ensure a safe online environment” for people in Australia.
The law sets out how platforms should judge what’s appropriate. They must weigh how well a measure reduces harm, whether it matches the level of risk, and how it affects security and users’ privacy. They can’t weigh expense. The law states that “the cost of the action or measures must not be taken into account.”
The duty also protects people who don’t use a service. The law states that a person “can be harmed” by online material “even if the person does not experience the material” as a user. That covers, for instance, someone whose fake nude image circulates on a platform they’ve never joined.
Who must comply?
The duty covers almost any service that people in Australia can reach online:
- social media, messaging apps, games and websites
- search engines and app stores
- hosting services and internet providers
- services that generate material using artificial intelligence (AI), including chatbots
- companies that make, supply, maintain or install equipment that connects people to the internet
The duty falls on the company that provides the service. For most services, it also falls on whoever has the most day-to-day control over it. The minister can exempt services that pose “little risk” to users, but must first seek the eSafety Commissioner’s advice.
What harms must platforms prevent?
The law sets out two lists. The first covers harms to everyone:
- Sexual abuse: Child sexual abuse material, grooming, sexual violence, fake nude images made without consent, and sharing or threatening to share intimate images
- Violence: Extreme violence or cruelty, explicit threats including rape and death threats, gender-based violence, and serious harassment
- Self-harm: Content that encourages suicide, self-harm, sadistic online exploitation or animal cruelty
- Terrorism and crime: Support for listed terrorist groups, praise of terrorist acts, violent extremist material, and incitement to serious crimes
The second list covers harms to children under 18. Platforms must also protect them from:
- pornography
- content that encourages eating disorders
- hostility towards women or gender equality
- content that glorifies crime or encourages dangerous stunts
- abuse, harassment and bullying
- material that “simulates emotional intimacy” and fosters a child’s dependence on it “in place of human relationships,” which would cover AI companion chatbots
- anything else that “may cause serious harm to children”
The law draws a line on the gender provision. Content doesn’t count as hostile to women “merely because it expresses disagreement with” feminism, gender equality, or laws and policies on gender. “This is not about disagreeing with feminism or about expressing an opinion,” Wells said.
What content falls outside the law?
The law excludes several kinds of material from its harm lists:
- professional news from outlets that follow editorial standards and stay independent of the people they cover
- material from public officials doing their jobs, and material used in court
- streaming shows and classified films and games, but not content users create inside games
- research, and literary, artistic or educational work that isn’t against the public interest
- material that protects public health or reduces harm
- material in the public interest
It also exempts lawful private messages between consenting adults.
What changes for under-16s?
Social media platforms must keep under-16s away from features that the law says “have negative behavioural impacts.” These include:
- recommendations based on information linked to a user’s account
- endless feeds that work only when a user is logged in
- like counts, view counts and follower notifications
- posts that disappear after a set time, such as stories
The minister can add features to this list, and decide which services count as social media, without Parliament passing a new law. In both cases, the minister must first seek the eSafety Commissioner’s advice.
Where children could see pornography, platforms must check users’ ages and offer at least two ways to do so. The law limits what platforms do with that data. They can use it only to check age, unless the user gives specific consent that they can easily withdraw. Afterwards, platforms must destroy the data. If a platform misuses or keeps the data, the law treats it as a breach of Australia’s Privacy Act.
What else must platforms do?
- Assess risks: Platforms must assess risks at least once a year and before any major change, including risks from addictive design. They must keep each assessment for six years and share it with the eSafety Commissioner on request.
- Offer user controls: The minister can require platforms to give users tools to shape their experience. The government plans to use this power for “My Feed, My Way.” It would let social media users aged 16 and over choose between a recommended feed and a feed of accounts they follow. The government is consulting on this rule separately.
- Make those controls easy to use: Platforms must keep these tools prominent, accessible and working. Using them can’t break the service or “reduce or impair user experience.”
- Handle complaints: The Commissioner can require some services to run complaint and dispute processes that meet set standards.
- Answer the regulator: The Commissioner can require platforms to name a point of contact.
How will the regulator enforce it?
The eSafety Commissioner can fine a company up to 5% of global turnover or A$109.2 million, whichever is higher. Individuals face fines of up to about A$21.8 million. The turnover-based penalty came from the government’s negotiations with the Australian Greens. “This has been a negotiating ask of the Greens,” Wells said.
The Commissioner can also order a platform to take specific steps to fix a breach. Ignoring that order carries a separate fine. The Commissioner can issue formal warnings and publish them on its website.
The law gives the regulator new ways to look inside platforms:
- Algorithms: The Commissioner can demand details of how recommendation systems work and send an expert to inspect them.
- Investigations: It can question people under oath and require regular transparency reports.
- Researchers: Approved researchers can access platform data.
- Test accounts: The Commissioner and approved researchers can create fake accounts to test platforms, even where a platform’s terms ban them. The Commissioner can also use them to check whether a service, including an AI tool, lets users generate illegal material.
The Commissioner must publish its enforcement priorities every year. It can also advise the minister on new kinds of harm and on services that concern it.
Can users sue?
Yes. Anyone who suffers harm can sue a social media, messaging, website or AI service if its breach “substantially contributes” to that harm. The law will “give individual Australians, as well as groups of Australians, the right to sue digital platforms when they breach their duty of care,” Wells said.
Courts can award damages, including for emotional distress, or order the platform to apologise. The costs rules favour users. A platform that loses pays the user’s legal costs. A user who loses doesn’t pay the platform’s costs, unless they sued without reasonable cause.
Users have until they turn 21, or six years after the harm, whichever is later. That lets a child harmed today sue as an adult. If the person dies, their family or estate can bring the case.
Wells expects few such cases. “We imagine that usage of the private right of action will remain fairly rare, as it has been in other jurisdictions,” she said.
What starts right away?
The law’s takedown changes apply from the day after royal assent:
- Fake nude apps: The eSafety Commissioner can order app stores and search engines to remove apps and websites built or mainly used to create fake nude images. It can order hosting providers to drop them and internet providers to block them.
- Intimate images: It can order search engines to stop linking to intimate images shared without consent within 24 hours.
- Faster takedowns: Platforms must act on removal notices within 24 hours, down from 48.
- Fewer hurdles for victims: Victims usually have to complain to the platform before the regulator steps in. The Commissioner can now skip that step if the platform has no working complaints system, or if complaining could cause further harm. It can also order reposted material removed without a fresh complaint.
- Higher penalties: A platform that ignores these notices faces a fine of up to about A$2.18 million.
Australia sets these fines in penalty units, a fixed dollar amount that the government indexes over time.
Why do critics call it censorship?
Critics argue that broad definitions of harm, backed by heavy fines, will push platforms to remove lawful speech. The US Embassy in Australia posted on X, quoting Ambassador David Brat:
“Vaguely defined ‘harms,’ backed by penalties of up to 5% of global revenue, will push platforms to censor lawful speech.”
“I think we would say there are points of difference, and we’re ironing them out,” Wells said in response.
Opposition leader Angus Taylor has argued that the framework could amount to government censorship.
The Australian Human Rights Commission (AHRC) warned that broad harm categories “may encourage services to restrict lawful material.” It asked Parliament to narrow the “may cause serious harm” catch-all. Parliament kept it.
Critics also question how much the law leaves to the minister. The minister can exempt services, decide what counts as social media and add features to the under-16 restrictions, all without new legislation.

German software giant SAP SE is considering eliminating at least 10,000 positions as part of a sweeping restructuring exercise aimed at repositioning its business for the artificial intelligence (AI) era, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter.
The proposed restructuring could affect at least 9% of SAP's global workforce. However, the final number of job cuts is yet to be determined and could change following negotiations with labour representatives, the report said.
The development follows two executive board reshuffles this year as Chief Executive Officer Christian Klein pushes ahead with an AI-first strategy. Two of SAP's six executive board members are set to leave the company in March.
"SAP continuously reviews its organization to ensure it remains aligned with its strategy and customer needs," the company told Bloomberg, declining to comment on potential job cuts.
According to the report, SAP is looking to overhaul its product development and sales operations as Klein seeks to integrate AI capabilities into the company's applications. All departments have been asked to identify potential areas for workforce reductions, with particular attention on product, engineering and sales teams.
Klein has already assumed most of the responsibilities of product chief Muhammad Alam, whose contract expires in March. Sales chief Thomas Saueressig also announced last week that he would leave SAP to take over as CEO of Ionos Group SE.
Its previous restructuring exercise, announced in 2024, saw around 10,000 positions eliminated at a cost of approximately 3 billion euros ($3.3 billion). The programme relied largely on voluntary departures and employee retraining. Overall headcount remained relatively stable as the company recruited for new roles.
SAP currently employs more than 110,000 people globally. In Germany, its largest employment market, the company's labour council secured an employment guarantee through 2028 earlier this year, Bloomberg reported.
"Our headcount has increased a little bit over the course of the year," SAP Chief Financial Officer Dominik Asam said at a Morgan Stanley conference last week, adding that he "would be really surprised" if that trend did not reverse.

The bank has told employees in India that it is centralising finance functions in key hubs including Chennai, Gurugram and Bengaluru, while ending such roles in other locations, including Hyderabad and Pune, Bloomberg reported.
HSBC Holdings is consolidating some finance support functions across its India operations as the Asia-focused lender steps up efforts to cut costs and accelerate the use of artificial intelligence.
The bank has told employees in India that it is centralising finance functions in key hubs including Chennai, Gurugram and Bengaluru, while ending such roles in other locations, including Hyderabad and Pune, Bloomberg reported.
The changes are limited to finance roles within HSBC’s global capability centres in India and are expected to affect several hundred positions, the people said. Employees will be offered support and the option to relocate, but HSBC will not provide additional cash incentives for the move, according to the report.
“As we simplify the bank, our focus remains on ensuring we have the right roles in the right locations to support the best customer outcomes,” an HSBC spokesperson said in a statement.
“We are taking the best of our people experience and combining this with emerging technologies to deliver outcomes that are better, faster, and safer for our clients,” the spokesperson said.
The move comes as HSBC CEO Georges Elhedery pushes a broader overhaul aimed at simplifying operations and reducing costs, with non-client-facing roles at global service centres expected to be among those most affected by the bank’s increased use of AI.
HSBC has been weighing job cuts of as many as 20,000 roles over the coming years as part of its AI-led restructuring, according to earlier Bloomberg reports. The potential reduction would amount to about 10% of the bank’s total workforce.
India is a key market for HSBC. The bank describes itself as the largest foreign lender in the country and generated $1.9 billion in pretax profit in the region in 2025. It had around 47,000 employees in India at the end of last year, including an estimated 42,500 working across its global capability centres.
HSBC is also targeting significant savings from its wider restructuring. In August, the lender raised its expected savings from the global restructuring programme to $2 billion from an earlier target of $1.5 billion. Elhedery has made simplifying the bank a central priority, saying earlier this year that he had been “ruthless about killing complexity” at HSBC.
The banking industry more broadly is reshaping its India operations as AI takes over tasks such as checking loan documents, reconciling accounts and writing basic code. Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan now employ more people in India than anywhere outside the US, while Standard Chartered plans to cut close to 8,000 support roles over four years.

deep-tech-265d291964.headline: A Stanford physicist drops an AI-assisted theory that has scientists at odds
deep-tech-265d291964.fulltext:
A scientist using ChatGPT's Astra model may have made progress on the biggest unsolved problems in physics.
And people have thoughts.
Venkatesa Chandrasekaran, a physicist at Stanford who is also employed at OpenAI, published a paper on Wednesday that claims to make strides on unifying two dueling theories that govern how the universe works.
Chandrasekaran said he arrived at several calculations "through detailed, back and forth collaboration with GPT-6 Astra" and spent about 400 million tokens — the units of data AI models process and how AI companies charge for compute.
On one side is general relativity: a blueprint for gravity masterminded by Albert Einstein in 1916. Broadly, it explains how planetary-sized objects bend the fabric of space and time, thereby creating the attractive force of gravity.
On the other side is quantum mechanics, a dense web of equations describing the behavior of particles smaller than the atom.
Though the two theories work in their respective domains, combining them into a unified framework has proven difficult. Physicists have spent about a century knocking their heads together to do that.
Chandrasekaran's paper, which has yet to be peer-reviewed, puts forth a mathematical theory that he says combines the theories in limited conditions.
The paper's claims — and the fact that OpenAI helped produce it — have roiled physicists and tech bros alike. Many called it bunk, while others said its propositions are illuminating.
Here's what smart people are saying.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman
In an X post, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman congratulated Chandrasekaran for his work and said he was one of the "earliest believers that we could use our then-current model to solve millennium prize problems."
"Being brilliant and also having correctly-placed confidence and courage to keep pushing on something that others don't think is possible is a very valuable thing and fairly rare," he wrote on X.
In the acknowledgments section of the paper, Chandrasekaran thanked Altman and others at the company for providing for his compute usage and "encouragement throughout the project."
Jonathan Oppenheim, physics professor
Jonathan Oppenheim, a professor of physics at University College London, poured cold water on the significance of Chandrasekaran's research.
In a Substack post, Oppenheim wrote the paper "doesn't even come close to establishing a quantum theory of gravity."
Oppenheim said the proposed unification was a false alarm and added that he dispatched a swarm of Claude agents to check it. He said the agents identified more than a dozen issues with the paper.
"We will keep getting false alarms like this one unless we find other ways to separate signal from slop," Oppenheim wrote.
Peter Woit, mathematician at Columbia University
Peter Woit, a mathematician at Columbia University, said the paper's findings did not check out or advance the field in any way. He called it a "publicity stunt" by OpenAI.
"It's more OpenAI worthless slop," Woit wrote on his website.
"For physics theory claims like this one, there's no reason to believe there's anything worthwhile there," he added.
Woit said he's reviewed thousands of papers making "similar claims" about quantum gravity and none have checked out.
"The only different thing about this one is that it's written by a machine and funded by a company that now has a track record of putting out misleading claims about physics," he wrote.
Hontas Farmer, theoretical astrophysicist
Hontas Farmer, a theoretical astrophysicist and professor at Chicago State University, said that while the paper checks out, it doesn't add anything to the conversation.
"It does not propose anything testable," she wrote on X. "It overlaps with many already published and or pre-printed ideas."
She said "AI boosters" are stoking hype for the paper, calling it "THE SOLUTION."
Nirmalya Kajuri, theoretical physicist
Nirmalya Kajuri, a theoretical physicist and science writer, said the paper doesn't solve quantum gravity, though it does make advancements toward the theory.
In a Substack post, he said in pre-AI days, a paper like this one wouldn't have gotten a lot of attention.
"It's an interesting project," he said. "Let us wait for another 400 milli tokens to see where it goes!"

New Delhi: The Philippines has fielded its BrahMos shore-based anti-ship missile battery in coordination with naval vessels during its annual joint defence exercise under the looming shadow of a potential China-Taiwan conflict.
The 10th iteration of AFP Joint Exercise (AJEX) DAGITPA 10-2026, held from 17 to 27 November, includes operations in Northern Luzon, Palawan, the National Capital Region, and the Western Command area, focusing on defending the country’s northern maritime approaches in the backdrop of China’s growing naval presence.
The Philippine Marine Corps’ Coastal Defence Regiment (CDR), according to the US Naval Institute (USNI), deployed the missile battery for a joint maritime strike exercise during DAGIT-PA.
The exercise marks the first confirmed field deployment of the BrahMos system during this series of drills, following earlier rehearsals during Balikatan 2026. It also involved movement of air-defence systems to Northern Luzon, naval escorts protecting military transport and special forces operations on Fuga Island.

The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) successfully concludes AJEX DAGITPA 10-2026, a ten-day joint and combined exercise held from November 17 to 27 across Northern Luzon and Palawan.
Bringing together the Philippine Army, Philippine… pic.twitter.com/aSNQ7scpiO
— Armed Forces of the Philippines (@TeamAFP) November 26, 2026
The Philippine military said the drills were aimed at strengthening its ability to secure vital maritime approaches, particularly the Luzon Strait.
Luzon Strait & its importance
Separating the northern Philippines from Taiwan and connecting the South China Sea with the Western Pacific, the Luzon Strait is an important passage for commercial shipping and naval movements.
The strait’s location makes it significant in the event of a conflict over Taiwan. Any escalation could affect the Philippines’ northern islands, including Batanes, and bring the country closer to the military consequences of a cross-strait confrontation. Manila has increased its military presence and conducted area-denial exercises with the US in the region.
Given the presence of commercial shipping routes and undersea communications cables, any military escalation around Taiwan can disrupt maritime traffic and affect regional trade. For the Philippines, the northern islands are particularly exposed to conflict spilling over from Taiwan.
This explains Manila’s increased military activity in northern Luzon and the Batanes region. Deploying BrahMos missiles during DAGIT-PA forms part of its effort to bolster coastal defences and deter hostile naval activity near these strategic approaches.
The Chinese reaction
While the BrahMos deployment has not received comparable attention from Chinese state media outlets, several commentators have examined the implications of India’s missile exports to Manila and the potential threat to Chinese naval vessels operating in the South China Sea.
In January 2022, India and the Philippines signed a $375-million contract for three BrahMos anti-ship missile batteries. The agreement made Manila the first foreign customer of the system, jointly developed by India’s Defence Research and Development Organisation and Russia’s NPO Mashinostroyeniya. The first delivery took place in April 2024.
Some of the commentators have questioned whether the Philippines has the monitoring, target tracking, communications and operational capabilities required to use the missiles effectively against higher technological opponents.
Their discussions point out that the missile’s performance would depend not only on its speed and range, but also on supporting capabilities such as electronic warfare, reliable communications and a clear operational picture.
India, according to a Reuters report in the first week of November, is in final-stage talks with the Philippines for a potential follow-on deal worth $700 million to $800 million. Manila is considering around five additional systems, involving nearly 60 missiles, and exploring ways to adapt the system to its local environment and logistical framework.
The recent deployment places the BrahMos missile at the centre of Manila’s efforts to strengthen coastal security, while highlighting India’s expanding footprint as an arms supplier in the Indo-Pacific region.

india-deep-tech-45a0b5dff9.fulltext:
Bank of England raises quantum computing concerns as Bitcoin, Ethereum prepare defenses
The Bank of England has identified the transition to quantum-resistant cryptography as an immediate financial stability priority, warning that advances in quantum computing could undermine the security systems protecting financial transactions, confidential information and digital signatures.
- Bank of England identifies quantum-resistant cryptography as an immediate priority.
- UK regulators target 2035 for completing the transition to quantum-resistant systems.
- Glassnode estimates 7.12 million BTC sits behind publicly exposed cryptographic keys.
- Ethereum researcher Justin Drake proposes December 2028 for its quantum transition.
- Bitcoin developers are evaluating BIP 360 and BIP 361 to address quantum threats.
In its November 26 Financial Stability Report, the central bank’s Financial Policy Committee (FPC) urged financial institutions to accelerate preparations for replacing vulnerable cryptographic systems, citing the considerable time and resources required to complete the transition.
“The immediate financial stability priority is an orderly transition to quantum-resistant cryptography,” the committee stated.
The warning coincides with ongoing efforts by Bitcoin and Ethereum developers to address vulnerabilities in the public-key cryptography used to authorize blockchain transactions.
Bank of England outlines quantum security migration timeline
The central bank’s report follows joint guidance published on November 19 by the Bank of England, the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA).
Although no cryptographically relevant quantum computer is known to exist, the regulators warned that financial institutions could already face risks from attackers collecting encrypted information for future decryption.
Known as harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks, the practice involves collecting confidential information that could become accessible once quantum computers develop sufficient capabilities to break existing encryption methods.
The regulators recommended that financial institutions identify where cryptography is used across their technology infrastructure, assess vulnerabilities in older systems and examine whether external service providers are prepared for the transition.
Following the National Cyber Security Centre’s recommendations, institutions are encouraged to complete their initial assessments and migration plans by the end of 2028. High-priority systems should transition by the end of 2031, with remaining systems moving to post-quantum cryptography by 2035.
In a November 4 statement, FCA Director of Specialists Mark Francis revealed that the regulator was testing a supervisory self-assessment tool with selected financial firms to measure their preparedness.
The FCA intends to expand the trial to additional institutions and identify common difficulties encountered during migration.
Over 7 million Bitcoin held behind publicly exposed keys
Similar cryptographic concerns have been discussed among Bitcoin developers because the network relies on elliptic-curve digital signatures, including ECDSA and Schnorr signatures, to authorize transactions.
A sufficiently powerful quantum computer could theoretically derive private keys from publicly available keys, allowing unauthorized transactions involving the associated Bitcoin holdings.
As crypto.news previously reported, blockchain analytics firm Glassnode estimated on November 10 that approximately 7.12 million BTC, representing 35.4% of Bitcoin’s issued supply, was held behind publicly visible keys.
Address reuse accounted for exposure equivalent to 25.8% of the issued supply, including 11.6% held on cryptocurrency exchanges. Glassnode had previously estimated exposed holdings at 6.04 million BTC in May.
Bitcoin developers have introduced several proposals to address these vulnerabilities, including Bitcoin Improvement Proposal 360, which introduces a transaction output structure known as Pay-to-Merkle-Root.
The proposal would reduce prolonged public-key exposure by removing Taproot’s key-path spending mechanism. However, protecting transactions against quantum attacks during the period between broadcasting and confirmation could require separate quantum-resistant signature schemes.
Developers are discussing BIP 361, which proposes gradually retiring existing signature systems. Neither proposal has been activated on Bitcoin’s mainnet.
Ethereum accelerates preparations for quantum-resistant cryptography
Ethereum faces similar vulnerabilities because its standard externally owned accounts use elliptic-curve signatures, allowing public keys to be recovered from signed transactions.
In a November 23 security update, Ethereum Foundation researcher Kev Wedderburn outlined plans to replace existing cryptographic systems across validator operations, user accounts and data availability infrastructure.
Validators would adopt hash-based signing keys, while wallet developers would introduce mechanisms allowing users to migrate to quantum-resistant signatures. Ethereum’s blobs, which temporarily store data for layer-2 networks, would transition to hash-based commitments.
The foundation has doubled its security team and identified advances in artificial intelligence as a more urgent concern than previously anticipated quantum computing threats.
During Devcon in Mumbai, Ethereum researcher Justin Drake proposed December 2028 as a target for completing the cryptographic transition. The foundation retains its internal 2029 deadline, with a formal review scheduled for January 2027.
Cryptocurrency custodians begin testing post-quantum security
Institutional cryptocurrency custodians face additional technical requirements because many use multi-party computation, which distributes transaction signing responsibilities among several independent participants.
Existing custody infrastructure may require substantial modifications to accommodate quantum-resistant signature algorithms while preserving distributed control over private keys.
In May, BitGo and Silence Laboratories demonstrated a simulated transaction using ML-DSA, a post-quantum signature standard, within a multi-party computation system.
Meanwhile, the UK regulators’ November guidance encourages financial institutions to assess the quantum readiness of third-party technology providers and determine whether their migration schedules are compatible with internal security plans.
The guidance outlines effective practices for financial firms but does not establish a separate quantum-resistance deadline specifically for cryptocurrency custodians.

EU plans €50 billion tech equity fund to boost quantum technology
November 25, 2026
The European Commission proposed a tech fund with a target size of €50 billion to boost quantum computing efforts. The bloc aims to keep up with the US and China in the global race.
The European Commission proposed a €50 billion ($54.73 billion) equity financing fund on Wednesday to boost artificial intelligence and quantum computing in Europe.
The draft "Quantum Act" aims to help Europe compete in a race against the United States and China.
"Quantum technologies will shape the future ‌of industry, security and innovation, and they will have a ‌profound impact on our societies. Europe needs to accelerate now," EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said in a statement.
"We want to build a fund and our target scale is now €50 billion," she said, calling it a "sufficient starting point."
Virkkunen introduced the officially named "Sovereign Tech Equity Fund" while presenting new rules to support Europe's quantum technology sector.
The new rules will push public authorities to favor European companies when giving public contracts and funding.
The European Union (EU) also wants to reduce its dependence on third countries amid concerns that US companies could use so-called "kill switches” to disable their products in Europe.
Why is quantum computing important?
Quantum computing technology is still at the early stages of development, with both the US and China competing to achieve dominance in the field.
While classical computers process data using bits — which are either 0 or 1 — quantum computers use qubits (quantum bits), which can exist in a blend of both states at once.
By using qubits, these machines could eventually solve complex problems much faster than today's supercomputers.
The EU expects the quantum computing to lead to breakthroughs in several areas, including drug development, earlier medical diagnoses or super-efficient batteries and even AI development.
Although quantum technology offers significant potential, it also poses cybersecurity risks, as it could undermine encryption and other safeguards for digital data at a time when governments are battling AI-driven cyberattacks.
Europe is home to one-third of the world's quantum companies
Around one-third of the world's quantum companies are based in the European Union, according to the Commission. Last year, public funding for quantum technologies reached €8.6 billion in the bloc, compared with €5.3 billion in the United States and €13.6 billion in China.
However, European quantum start-ups have attracted €1.1 billion in private funding so far, compared with €7 billion in the United States.
The EU launched its "quantum Europe" strategy in July 2025, aiming to be a global leader in quantum technologies by 2030.
The bloc is already a global leader in quantum research but it falls short when it comes to transforming this into viable commercial opportunities.
The draft legislation must be negotiated with EU member states and the European Parliament in the upcoming months before it can be law.

(Bloomberg) -- The dollar is poised for its longest monthly winning streak in two years as a rupture in the artificial intelligence trade and rising interest rates spur demand for safe-haven assets.
The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index is up 1.8% in November, putting it on track for a third straight month of gains. The greenback has strengthened against all of its Group-of-10 peers, including the Japanese yen and the Swiss franc.
A slump in technology stocks, coupled with robust economic growth and elevated inflation, propelled the dollar higher over the past three months. The greenback held near its strongest level since April 2025 in early Asian trading after jumping in pre-holiday US hours on Wednesday, as the Nasdaq 100 index briefly plunged into a bear market and a measure of underlying inflation hit the highest since 2023.
“It’s a pretty good dollar storm,” said Steven Englander, co-head of FX research and North America macro strategy at Standard Chartered.
Market repricing for a more hawkish Federal Reserve also supported the dollar this month, according to Sarah Ying, CIBC’s head of FX strategy.
Traders are fully pricing a 25 basis point interest rate hike next month for the Fed, and are betting on the possibility of two additional increases by the middle of next year. Policymakers have been flagging the need for more tightening, with some calling for lifting rates at successive meetings, while others are open to the possibility of raising by more than the usual quarter percentage point in December.
Some Wall Street strategists expect the dollar rally to extend into 2027, pointing to the very AI spending binge that’s making stock markets jittery as a driver of US economic growth and capital flows. The greenback has benefited from overseas investors converting local currencies to buy shares of US companies that use the tech.
“The US economy is booming and inflation is still moving away from the target,” said Win Thin, chief economist at Bank of Nassau 1982. “The Fed needs to hike rates to help cool the economy, perhaps in both December and January. That’s dollar positive.”
The dollar’s latest surge has won over short-dated options traders, but conviction further out has weakened over the past two months. The divergence suggests investors are positioning for dollar strength into early 2027 while becoming less willing to extend bullish bets much further.
The latest equities sell-off has raised concerns about the longevity of the AI boom, fueling sharp swings in global markets. In such an environment, the dollar has become “the haven of choice,” according to Goldman Sachs, while MUFG believes that the prospect of higher rates is also helping the currency.
“Weakness in the US equity market is taking place at a time when there is building evidence of strengthening cyclical growth momentum in the US, which is encouraging a stronger US dollar as a safe haven play,” said Lee Hardman, senior currency analyst at MUFG.
“The strength of the US economy supports the view of investors that returns are likely to remain higher in the US even if they are currently being challenged by the recent sell-off in US assets,” he said.

The world's richest person has made a commitment to every child in the United States. SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk pledged that every child in the country would receive two shares in the space and AI company, which raised about $85.7 billion (€78.4bn) when it went public in June 2026.
"Every child in America will receive two SpaceX shares, one from the company and one from me personally," Musk said in a post on X, the social media platform owned by SpaceX.
SpaceX said it would give one newly issued Class A share to each currently active Trump Account, a tax-advantaged investment account for children, and that Musk would match its contribution.
SpaceX will transfer its shares in December, Musk said. He said he would transfer his own shares in June 2027, when restrictions on transferring them expire.
In October, Musk promised that every child in the US would receive one SpaceX share, adding that it would be "the first of many."
The value of the pledge is unknown. It depends on the share price, but also on how many Trump Accounts are eligible for this offer.
To receive shares through the programme, parents or guardians must claim and activate their child's Trump Account. The US government provides a one-off $1,000 (€914) contribution for eligible US citizens born from 2025 through 2028.
The money is generally invested in low-cost funds that track the US stock market, and withdrawals are usually restricted until the year the child turns 18.
The White House said nearly 70 million accounts had been created by October. It is unclear how many have been activated.
At Wednesday's closing price of $127.44, two shares were worth $254.88. The pledge would be worth about $17.8 billion (€16.3bn) if 70 million accounts received both shares.
