HOW DOES A 17% TARIFF RATE COMPARE?
The proposed 17% rate contingent on a trade deal is a little lower than rates planned for many key countries with which India competes, potentially giving Indian exporters a competitive advantage.
The Trump administration has proposed a rate of 18% for Bangladesh, Cambodia and Indonesia. It is also planning a 20% rate for Vietnam provided the Southeast Asian nation strikes a trade deal.
Also Read: India, China and others aren't taking Trump's latest tariff salvo lying down
China too faces a rate of 20%, which complies with a US-China trade truce that expires on January 10. But if the truce unravels, China's rate would rise to 40%. China's 20% rate would be added to duties of roughly 25% imposed during Trump's first term.
The potential 17% rate for India is also a notch lower than the 18% agreed by the US and India in a framework for a trade deal in February. That was before the US Supreme Court invalidated President Donald Trump's use of emergency powers to impose sweeping tariffs globally, leading to the current 10% baseline rate.
WHAT IS THE US RATIONALE AND HOW HAS NEW DELHI RESPONDED?
The US has accused India of unreasonable trade practices including inadequate labour protections, financial repression, market access barriers and failure to address global excess capacity.
India's trade ministry said on late Wednesday it was examining the notice from the US Trade Representative's office. India had told the US during its investigation that it had no structural excess capacity in any sector, it added.
WHY HAVE TRADE TALKS STRETCHED OUT SO LONG?
India began talks with the US on a trade deal in February 2025 but unlike other nations, it has yet to come to an agreement.
Complications include a new US law that paves the way for up to 100% tariffs on Indian goods because of New Delhi's purchases of Russian oil. However, recent months have seen those purchases decline due to a fall in global crude prices and increased supplies from Saudi Arabia.
Bilateral ties between India and the US have been rocky this past year. Events that hurt relations include a US military attack on a ship off Oman that killed three Indian seafarers and India's rejection of Trump's repeated claim that he has brokered a ceasefire between India and Pakistan.
WHAT IS AT STAKE?
The US is India's largest export market and exports have so far been resilient.
India's exports of goods to the United States surged 14.5% to $59.5 billion during the April-October period.
India says many of its largest export categories to the US, including generic pharmaceuticals and smartphones, are not subject to the current 10% levy.
But analysts say that failure to strike a trade deal could hurt businesses, dent market sentiment and hurt the Indian currency, which in October fell close to record lows.
India is particularly keen to keep dairy, poultry, rice, wheat and other farm products outside the scope of market-opening commitments.

agritech-b5469092b5.headline: India's Q2 GDP Growth Seen Easing to 7.6% as Weak Monsoon Hits Farms
agritech-b5469092b5.fulltext:
Industry Odisha Bureau, Nov 26: India's economic growth likely slowed slightly to 7.6% in the July-September quarter. The figure is the median estimate from a Mint poll of 14 economists. It compares with 7.8% growth in the April-June quarter of FY27. A deficient monsoon and uneven rural demand are expected to have dragged on output. Official GDP data for the second quarter will be released on 30 November.
FY27 is India's financial year, running from April 2026 to March 2027. Forecasts in the poll range from 7.2% to 8%. If the median estimate holds, growth will stay above 7% for a fifth straight quarter. It would, however, fall short of the 8.1% expansion recorded a year earlier. Persistent external headwinds have also weighed on the economy.
Agriculture is expected to have borne the heaviest blow. Southwest monsoon rains were about 13% below the long-period average (LPA). The LPA is the benchmark used to judge a normal monsoon. Kharif sowing, the main summer crop planting season, was marginally lower than a year ago. Falling real rural wages and weaker tractor sales also point to softer village demand.
Rating agency Icra expects GDP growth to ease to 7.5% from 7.8%. Its chief economist, Aditi Nayar, said sub-par monsoons likely hurt agricultural output. She cited lower kharif sowing and a probable adverse effect on crop yields. Icra forecasts agricultural gross value added growth to slow sharply to just 0.2%.
Industry and services, however, appear to have cushioned the slowdown. Industrial production data showed manufacturing output rose 8.1% year-on-year during the quarter. Strong credit growth and healthy auto sales signal resilient domestic demand. Corporate profitability and demand for capital goods also supported factory activity.
CareEdge expects growth to hold steady at 7.6%. It cited robust high-frequency indicators, which track economic activity in near real time. The agency also analysed around 1,600 listed non-financial companies. Their revenue and profitability grew by more than 20% year-on-year.
Services are expected to remain the main engine of growth. Financial, real estate and professional services are likely to have led the sector. But contracting mining output and subdued air traffic may have offset some gains.
Economists will also watch the gap between GDP and gross value added (GVA). GVA measures the value of output produced across sectors of the economy. GDP adds net indirect taxes, meaning taxes minus subsidies, to that figure. Nirmal Bang estimates second-quarter GVA growth at 8%, against GDP growth of 7.6%. CareEdge projects GVA growth of 7.7% alongside its 7.6% GDP forecast. When GVA outpaces GDP, net indirect taxes are growing more slowly than output.
The data will also test how durable India's domestic demand has been. Economists expect growth to moderate in the second half of FY27. They point to agricultural stress, weaker rural demand and rising input costs. A less favourable statistical base from last year's strong growth could also weigh. The 30 November release will show whether industry can keep offsetting farm weakness.

A drone attack in Kuwait killed two Italian technicians working on an air defence system on Thursday (November 276, 2026), marking the first fatal strike in the Gulf state for months.
Also read | A changing Washington, a shift in U.S.-Israel ties
Both Italy and Kuwait confirmed the deaths, blaming the attack on Iran. But Tehran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi insisted in calls to his Kuwaiti and Italian counterparts that it was not behind the deadly strike.
Iran has in the last week ratcheted up attacks on Kuwait and Gulf neighbour Bahrain while it continues to fight the United States for control of the contested Strait of Hormuz.
"Around 2:00 p.m. today, several Iranian-made drones targeted Kuwaiti military installations, including an air-defence detection station where two Italian technicians from Rheinmetall were working," Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani told the Senate.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni took to social media to offer her condolences.
"My thoughts are with all those affected by the attack and their families," she wrote on X.
But Iran was quick to refute the allegations that it was behind the deadly attack.
Mr. Araghchi held phone calls with both his Kuwaiti counterpart Jarrah Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah and Italian counterpart Antonio Tajani to deny Tehran's involvement, according to Iran's state TV and Foreign Ministry.
In his call with Tajani, "Araghchi stated that Iran had no role or involvement whatsoever in the occurrence of this event," the Iranian Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
Iran's top diplomat added that Tehran was prepared to cooperate with Kuwait and Italy to "determine the origin of the incident", the ministry said.
He also offered a joint probe in his call with Mr. Al-Sabah, state TV reported.
Armed forces spokesperson Abolfazl Shekarchi had earlier refuted the claims that Iran was involved and blamed false flag operations by Israel and the United States for the attack, without providing evidence.
"No military or offensive operations have been conducted by the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran in the region," he said, state TV reported.
But EU chief Ursula von der Leyen called for more pressure on Tehran after the deaths.
"We must step up pressure on Iran to put an end to these unacceptable attacks against its neighbours and our partners in the Gulf," she wrote on social media.
The Kuwaiti Defence Ministry had earlier said that at least four people were injured in the incident, saying several drones had targeted an unspecified, vital location in the country.
Air defences
The attack comes days after Kuwait activated its air defences last week to counter drone strikes launched by Iran — the first since early September.
The conflict — which began with U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February — has seen the Gulf states caught in the crossfire, with US military facilities and energy installations on their soil targeted.
The United States and Iran are in a standoff over the vital Strait of Hormuz, with the U.S. military working to escort ships transiting the waterway in defiance of Tehran's attempts to close the waterway.
Further south, the war between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis continued to rage, following a week that saw the two sides trade heavy blows.
The Saudi-led military coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said the Iran-backed group struck a refinery in southern Saudi Arabia's Jazan, which state media said killed one person and triggered a temporary shutdown of some operations.
It marked the latest in a series of barrages targeting major energy installations in the kingdom.
The coalition also claimed to have destroyed a ballistic missile launcher in Houthi territory that was used in the attack on the refinery.
The exchanges between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen have become near-daily in the country's revived civil war, which first began more than a decade ago.
Later Thursday (November 26), Houthi media, citing their Health Ministry, published figures saying 19 civilians had been killed in the past 48 hours by "Saudi-led aggression".
Earlier, the coalition, which backs Yemen's internationally recognised government, said its forces had intercepted two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards the Saudi capital of Riyadh overnight, where residents and an AFP journalist heard an explosion.

Ukraine says Russia hits two grain ships carrying 100,000 tonnes near Odesa
Russia attacked two foreign grain ships near Odesa, Ukraine said, as grain exports from the country's Black Sea ports remain disrupted by security risks and soaring insurance costs.
Russia attacked two foreign cargo ships carrying more than 100,000 metric tons of grain overnight near Ukraine's Black Sea port of Odesa, Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergiy Koretskyi said on Thursday.
Koretskyi did not say where the grain originated nor where the vessels had loaded their cargo.
Ukraine has said grain shipments from its key Black Sea ports around Odesa have all but stopped since late July after Russia sharply intensified attacks on grain terminals and merchant vessels.
Russia says it does not attack civilian targets.
Before the escalation, the three ports in the Odesa hub handled about 90% of Ukraine's agricultural and metallurgical exports.
Kyiv has not formally banned port operations, but shipowners have avoided the ports because of security risks, while soaring insurance costs have deterred traders.
President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said earlier this year that shipments from Odesa ports were taking place only intermittently, while Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskiy has said no exports were moving through them.
Analysts' data show that Ukraine's state railway continues to transport grain towards Black Sea ports.
Consultancy APK-Inform reported this week that 429 grain wagons were dispatched towards Odesa between November 12 and November 18, four times the level recorded a week earlier.
Ukraine does not publish official data on shipments from its Black Sea ports, saying agricultural exports have instead been redirected to Danube River ports or moved by rail across land borders with eastern European countries.
Official data showed Ukraine had exported 7.6 million tons of grain so far in the 2026/27 July-June season, down from 11.5 million tons in the same period a year earlier.

Kharif output in 2026-27 dips amid deficient monsoon, but still better than 5-year average; 2025-26 crop year, however, reports record output of foodgrains
Vishwa Mohan / TNN / Updated: Nov 26, 2026, 20:18 IST
Recent preliminary estimates from the agriculture ministry indicate a decline in kharif foodgrain production caused by insufficient rainfall.
NEW DELHI: Deficient monsoon rainfall this year impacted the kharif (summer sown) crop output, with the agriculture ministry’s first advance estimates for the 2026-27 crop year, released on Thursday, showing a dip compared to last year. But the output is still estimated to be better than the five-year average (normal) production.On the other hand, the ministry’s final estimates for the 2025-26 crop year put the overall foodgrain production at an all-time high of 378 million tonnes (MT), up about 5.8% from a year earlier, with India figuring at the top in the world in producing five crops such as paddy, pulses, jute, millets and spices.The output of 2025-26, backed by good monsoon rainfall last year, made India the largest producer of paddy in the world, ahead of China, for the second consecutive year. The country ranks second after China in wheat, cotton, groundnut, fruits and vegetables, and second after Brazil in sugarcane production. Major crops such as paddy, wheat and maize reported all-time high output in 2025-26.The current year (2026-27), however, shows some concerns. Total kharif foodgrain production is estimated at 167 MT, which is 5% lower compared to the final output figure of the seasonal crops in the previous year.
Though the overall kharif output is estimated above the five-year average, major crops such as paddy, maize, pulses and oilseeds are expected to decline.“These are very preliminary estimates and are subject to change as the year goes by,” said Union agriculture minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan while releasing these estimates. Advance estimates are revised as the season progresses, based on the inputs provided by states.
He admitted that the crop sowing had been affected this year by the El Niño-induced deficient rainfall, noting that the low soil moisture and drought-like conditions in major agricultural states such as Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh had also affected the sowing of crops including paddy, maize, tur, soybean and cotton.“Despite these difficult conditions, the determination and resilience of farmers, the support provided through government schemes and the climate-resilient crop varieties developed by scientists had helped sustain agricultural production,” said Chouhan while flagging the estimated kharif output which is expected to be nearly 9.8 MT higher than the average of the last five years.
Vishwa Mohan is Senior Editor at The Times of India. He writes on environment, climate change, agriculture, water resources and clean energy, tracking policy issues and climate diplomacy. He has been covering Parliament since 2003 to see how politics shaped up domestic policy and India’s position at global platform. Before switching over to explore sustainable development issues, Vishwa had covered internal security and investigative agencies for more than a decade.

agritech-f0aa9ed1db.headline: From Gulf war to fertiliser security: India’s ₹54000 crore bet on domestic urea production
agritech-f0aa9ed1db.fulltext:
The fertiliser crisis triggered by the Gulf war has exposed a strategic vulnerability in Indian agriculture: the country’s ability to sustain food production remains partly dependent on industrial facilities, energy supplies and shipping routes beyond its borders.The disruption of fertiliser supply chains across West Asia has reinforced the urgency of expanding domestic production capacity and insulating Indian farmers from geopolitical shocks.The government’s November 25 approval of six gas-based urea manufacturing projects, involving an estimated investment of ₹54,000 crore, represents a significant intervention in this direction. Together, the projects will add 76.2 lakh tonnes to India’s annual urea manufacturing capacity, potentially reducing import dependence, strengthening fertiliser availability and improving the resilience of agricultural supply chains.The projects, approved under the National Investment Policy for Urea (NIPU)-2026, cover six locations: Chennai, Nangal, Shahjahanpur, Panagarh, Gadepan and Jagdishpur. With participation from public sector enterprises, cooperatives and private manufacturers, the programme combines industrial expansion with the technological modernisation of ageing fertiliser manufacturing infrastructure. Each project will have an annual installed capacity of 12.7 lakh tonnes.The scale of India's import vulnerability is evident from the mismatch between domestic production and consumption. According to the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, India consumes approximately 400 lakh tonnes of urea annually, against domestic production of 293.30 lakh tonnes in 2025–26. Although production has expanded considerably from 225 lakh tonnes in 2014–15, rising agricultural demand has constrained progress towards self-sufficiency.The Gulf war aggravated this structural vulnerability. West Asia is a major centre of global fertiliser manufacturing, benefiting from abundant natural gas reserves and relatively low production costs. Disruptions to maritime trade, energy supplies and manufacturing operations in the region have complicated fertiliser procurement. For India, the consequences extend beyond the availability of imported urea. Higher international fertiliser and natural gas prices also translate into greater subsidy expenditure for the government.The procurement of fertilisers during periods of geopolitical instability is particularly challenging because agricultural demand is seasonal. Delays in shipments during critical sowing periods can affect crop productivity and rural incomes. Domestic manufacturing provides greater control over production schedules, inventories and distribution, although it cannot entirely eliminate exposure to international energy markets.The government's investment strategy builds on the experience of the New Investment Policy of 2012, which facilitated the establishment of six manufacturing units, including facilities at Ramagundam, Gorakhpur, Sindri and Barauni. The new policy seeks to improve the commercial viability of fertiliser manufacturing by providing a return-on-equity band of 12–16%, alongside mechanisms to mitigate foreign exchange risks and improve transparency in production costs.An important dimension of the latest approvals is the replacement of technologically obsolete manufacturing infrastructure. The Madras Fertilizers facility in Chennai is over six decades old, while National Fertilizers Limited's Nangal facility has been operating for more than five decades. Replacing energy-intensive plants with modern facilities could lower natural gas consumption per tonne of urea, improve operational safety and reduce manufacturing costs.However, the combined installed capacity of 76.2 lakh tonnes should not be interpreted as an equivalent net addition to domestic production, since some projects will replace existing facilities. The actual reduction in import dependence will depend on commissioning schedules, capacity utilisation, retirement of older plants and future consumption patterns.There is also a fundamental limitation to India's strategy of achieving fertiliser self-sufficiency through gas-based manufacturing. Natural gas is both a feedstock and an energy source for urea production. With India dependent on imported liquefied natural gas to meet a significant portion of its requirements, expanding domestic urea production could partially shift import dependence from finished fertilisers to energy feedstocks.Diversification of natural gas procurement, expansion of domestic gas production and improvements in manufacturing efficiency must therefore accompany the capacity expansion programme. Over the longer term, advances in green ammonia production using renewable hydrogen could provide an alternative pathway, subject to improvements in commercial viability.The supply-side intervention must also be accompanied by reforms in fertiliser consumption. India’s heavily subsidised urea pricing regime has encouraged excessive nitrogen application and discouraged balanced use of phosphorus, potassium and other nutrients. Indiscriminate urea consumption contributes to soil degradation, groundwater contamination, declining nutrient-use efficiency and greenhouse gas emissions.The policy challenge is to reduce excessive consumption without imposing additional financial burdens on farmers. Soil testing, precision agriculture, crop-specific nutrient recommendations and gradual rationalisation of fertiliser subsidies could help achieve this objective. Improvements in nutrient-use efficiency would reduce import requirements and subsidy expenditure without compromising agricultural productivity.The ₹54,000 crore investment programme is, therefore, as much an exercise in economic and strategic security as in agricultural policy. It offers an opportunity to modernise India's fertiliser industry, reduce exposure to volatile international markets and strengthen the foundations of food security.Its ultimate success, however, cannot be measured exclusively in tonnes of additional urea produced. India must simultaneously reduce the energy intensity of manufacturing, diversify feedstock supplies and correct distortions in fertiliser consumption. Genuine fertiliser security requires not only the capacity to produce more urea but also the ability to achieve higher agricultural productivity with less of it.

work-careers-4fc36af988.fulltext:
IBM ends US visa sponsorship; India workers face 80% pay cut or job loss
IBM employees affected by the decision have three weeks to choose between overseas relocation and leaving the company, with most available consulting positions listed in India
Listen to This Article
IBM is ending US visa and green card sponsorship for most positions in IBM Consulting, its largest division, which employs more than 150,000 people. Employees affected by the decision have been given the option of relocating to an IBM role outside the US or leaving the company by the end of the year, Bloomberg first reported, citing a document shared with managers in the division.
The decision is particularly challenging for H-1B visa holders, who have reportedly been given just three weeks to choose between relocating and leaving the company, according to accounts posted by IBM employees on anonymous workplace forum Blind.
Employees who do not accept an overseas position will receive three months' severance, with December 31 set as their last working day. Several employees reportedly learnt about the decision during meetings described as one-on-one 'career syncs' with their managers.
One IBM employee wrote on Blind that relocating to India could result in an estimated 80 per cent pay cut.
"I got pulled into a surprise meeting with my manager and was told I have just three weeks to choose between taking an 80 per cent pay cut to relocate to India or losing my job by December 31," the employee wrote.
Also Read
"I've spent years building my career here, working long hours for IBM clients, paying taxes and building a life in the US. Now I'm being told to either uproot everything or walk away with just three months of severance," the post added.
The relocation options also appear to be concentrated in India. On November 19, IBM's careers portal listed 1,278 consulting vacancies outside the US, of which 1,125 were in India, 23 in Singapore and 18 in the UK. The portal listed 89 consulting openings in the US.
Federal records show that IBM had just over 1,600 H-1B petitions approved in fiscal year 2026, compared with more than 2,000 in FY2025 and nearly 3,000 in FY2024. These figures cover the entire company, rather than IBM Consulting alone, and include petitions for extensions of existing employees.
IBM's 2025 annual report put its total workforce at 264,300 employees across the company and its wholly owned subsidiaries.
Trump administration's H-1B visa crackdown
The move comes amid increased scrutiny of foreign-worker hiring by the Donald Trump administration.
Last month, the administration suspended Microsoft, Adobe and several major outsourcing companies, including Cognizant, Infosys and Tata Consultancy Services, from participating in the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) process, Reuters reported. PERM is a key step in the process through which employers sponsor foreign workers for employment-based green cards.
Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling announced the suspensions. Microsoft has publicly defended its recruitment of international talent.
In September 2025, the White House announced a one-time fee of $100,000 on new H-1B petitions. The measure has since faced legal challenges. The administration has also proposed changes to the annual H-1B lottery system that would give preference to employers offering higher salaries.
Indian professionals are particularly exposed to changes in US immigration policy. Indian nationals account for roughly three-quarters of H-1B visas issued, while their wait for employment-based green cards can stretch over several decades, according to the National Foundation for American Policy.

science-mind-5e99dc763a.headline: Lower central dark matter densities in nearby galaxies than predicted by simulations
science-mind-5e99dc763a.fulltext:
Abstract
Baryonic feedback in hydrodynamical simulations is typically invoked to alleviate the core–cusp problem in dwarf galaxies. Yet baryonic processes also induce adiabatic contraction of dark matter (DM), producing overly steep density profiles and excessively high DM fractions in the inner regions of massive galaxies. The DM distribution of galaxies across a wide stellar mass range is therefore a critical test for such simulations, but a comprehensive benchmark has remained absent. Here we consistently measure the DM distribution from galaxy centres out to radii of 20–50 kpc for 136 nearby galaxies that together span the local mass–size relation over the stellar mass interval 109–1011.5 M⊙. We identify central regions with lower DM densities relative to Λ cold dark matter simulation expectations, whose extent grows from about 10 to >50 kpc as stellar mass increases from 1010 to 1011 M⊙. Although their physical origin remains unclear, these low-dark-matter regions are clearly indicated by the data. Our results provide an important observational benchmark for future hydrodynamical simulations that explore alternative DM models and feedback processes.

Nvidia halts server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia after tighter US export controls
Key Points
- The Financial Times reported that Nvidia told partners including Dell and Supermicro to halt server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia. New US export controls are designed to stop Chinese companies from bypassing sales bans through foreign cloud providers.
- Dealers have listed an unusually large number of Nvidia GPUs for sale as a result of the rules, CNBC reported. The supply includes thousands of B300 chips originally intended for data centers with Chinese rental customers.
- Cloud providers in Southeast Asia now have 90 days to apply for a license, a requirement one executive said has led to "chaos." Banks have already halted about $500 million in loans to Singapore-based provider Aolani for a planned deal with ByteDance, the Financial Times reported.
The US is closing cloud loopholes that give Chinese companies access to AI chips. Nvidia is responding by halting shipments to four countries, while thousands of high-performance processors are looking for new buyers on the secondary market.
Nvidia has told manufacturing partners such as Dell and Supermicro to stop shipping servers to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia. The Financial Times reported the halt, citing three people familiar with the matter. It isn't clear whether the pause is only temporary, according to the report.
The move follows tighter US export controls from the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security. The rules aim to stop Chinese companies from getting around existing sales bans by renting computing power from foreign cloud providers. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC the goal was to block indirect access, including smuggling through Southeast Asia and remote access via data centers in third countries.
Thousands of B300 chips hit the market as cloud providers face chaos
The controls are already affecting the hardware market, CNBC reported. Since the announcement, dealers have listed an unusually large number of Nvidia GPUs for sale. Jack Duhamel, president of the AI infrastructure marketplace GPU Mart, and two other insiders confirmed to CNBC that the surge is a direct result of the new rule. According to the report, sellers are looking for new buyers for hardware, including thousands of B300 chips, one of Nvidia's most advanced models. Those chips were originally intended for data centers with Chinese rental customers.
The rollout has created significant uncertainty in Southeast Asia, the Financial Times reported. Cloud providers have 90 days to apply for a license and prove that no restricted companies are among their end users. One cloud provider executive described the situation to the paper as chaos, saying there was no guidance on how to apply.
The fallout is also hitting major infrastructure projects. Banks have halted about $500 million in loans to Singapore-based cloud provider Aolani, which planned to rent computing power to TikTok parent ByteDance, the Financial Times reported. ByteDance could now pull out of the deal.

German software giant SAP SE is considering eliminating at least 10,000 positions as part of a sweeping restructuring exercise aimed at repositioning its business for the artificial intelligence (AI) era, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter.
The proposed restructuring could affect at least 9% of SAP's global workforce. However, the final number of job cuts is yet to be determined and could change following negotiations with labour representatives, the report said.
The development follows two executive board reshuffles this year as Chief Executive Officer Christian Klein pushes ahead with an AI-first strategy. Two of SAP's six executive board members are set to leave the company in March.
"SAP continuously reviews its organization to ensure it remains aligned with its strategy and customer needs," the company told Bloomberg, declining to comment on potential job cuts.
According to the report, SAP is looking to overhaul its product development and sales operations as Klein seeks to integrate AI capabilities into the company's applications. All departments have been asked to identify potential areas for workforce reductions, with particular attention on product, engineering and sales teams.
Klein has already assumed most of the responsibilities of product chief Muhammad Alam, whose contract expires in March. Sales chief Thomas Saueressig also announced last week that he would leave SAP to take over as CEO of Ionos Group SE.
Its previous restructuring exercise, announced in 2024, saw around 10,000 positions eliminated at a cost of approximately 3 billion euros ($3.3 billion). The programme relied largely on voluntary departures and employee retraining. Overall headcount remained relatively stable as the company recruited for new roles.
SAP currently employs more than 110,000 people globally. In Germany, its largest employment market, the company's labour council secured an employment guarantee through 2028 earlier this year, Bloomberg reported.
"Our headcount has increased a little bit over the course of the year," SAP Chief Financial Officer Dominik Asam said at a Morgan Stanley conference last week, adding that he "would be really surprised" if that trend did not reverse.

ai-958b4d502f.headline: The questions Jensen Huang and Nvidia will still have to answer about Megaspeed
ai-958b4d502f.fulltext:
Jensen Huang’s return as CEO to Nvidia hasn’t eased the scrutiny the company faces. The chipmaker still needs to address multiple inquiries into allegations that its advanced GPUs were smuggled into China by a customer, the Singapore-based data center operator Megaspeed, in violation of U.S. export rules designed to slow China’s development of frontier AI models.
The central question for investigators is what Nvidia knew about where those chips ended up and whether Huang’s affair with a Megaspeed executive gave the company reason to doubt Megaspeed’s assurances. Huang’s return doesn’t settle that. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche has suggested Nvidia isn’t a target of an investigation, but California’s attorney general and Congress are pressing ahead, and the Securities and Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating, too.
The U.S. government opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 and requested information from Nvidia about its billions of dollars in sales to the company, concerned that some of the chips Megaspeed bought for data center projects in Malaysia were in fact being diverted to China. Singapore also began investigating similar allegations in 2025. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.
Diversion of this kind would be a fairly routine issue for a company like Nvidia, whose in-demand chips are the targets of smugglers and resellers. When it comes to compliance and liability for export-control violations, Nvidia and other chip sellers need assurances that the end users of their chips are obeying the rules. However, they also cannot ignore other information that might call the reliability of those assurances into question, export-control attorneys told TechCrunch.
And that’s why Jensen Huang’s affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang was such a problem for Nvidia, likely even more so than her alleged role as a source for Chinese intelligence agencies. If Nvidia personnel, from lower-level employees up to the CEO, had reason to believe that statements from Megaspeed weren’t reliable, the attorneys said, that would increase the company’s legal risk.
“Government investigators likely would want to know, notwithstanding whatever formal assurances were exchanged between the parties, what anyone at Nvidia actually knew about the end use and end users of the chips,” Dan Fisher-Owens, an attorney at the firm Berliner Corcoran & Rowe, told TechCrunch last week.
The concern Nvidia’s board faced when it decided to oust Huang is that he knew more about what Megaspeed was doing with Nvidia’s products than was reflected in any of the compliance statements. The Wall Street Journal reported that Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, were part of a network of businesses that funneled chips to a company in Shanghai. Kang also reportedly introduced his wife to Jensen Huang, whom he had known for a decade.
On Monday, the U.S. government added Megaspeed and its affiliates to a list of companies restricted from U.S. trade due to national security concerns. The U.S. also issued new rules last week barring large data centers that purchase U.S. chips from serving customers in China and other nations seen as problematic by the U.S. government. Nvidia, meanwhile, said it would stop selling licensed chips to China and laid out plans to hire its first compliance officer and create a new board committee focused on export controls.
Nvidia’s board said it reinstated Huang on Monday after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that left it confident his return posed no national security risk. President Donald Trump later said he called into the meeting to give them that assurance.
In a news conference Tuesday, Blanche said that Nvidia was “a good corporate citizen” and suggested it is not the target of an investigation, but Blanche declined to answer questions about the government’s investigation into Megaspeed, which the Justice Department said was ongoing as recently as last week.
“When you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don’t know what you’re talking about,” Blanche said.
Other authorities may be more demanding. Nvidia faces investigations by California Attorney General Rob Bonta and, reportedly, the SEC, both tied to its corporate disclosures. While many details of the investigation still aren’t known, short sellers complained about the company’s decision to stop breaking out its exports to Singapore in financial filings after journalists raised concerns about chip diversion.
Members of Congress from both parties say they want answers from Nvidia, with many citing alarm about China and some questioning the White House’s role in Huang’s return. Three committees in the House of Representatives will privately interview Huang and Nvidia’s top lawyer, Tim Teter, next week. Teter reportedly intervened in the Department of Commerce’s investigation of Megaspeed last year.
“We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of Nvidia products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary’s AI capabilities,” the Republican chairs of House committees focused on foreign affairs, intelligence, and China said in a joint statement.
Rep. Brian Mast, the chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has also demanded that the Department of Commerce share extensive data regarding its investigation into chip smuggling, including by Megaspeed and its affiliates.
The Senate Banking Committee will also question Huang in a public hearing on December 3.
“Mr. Huang, Nvidia executives, and the company’s board still owe Congress answers about the company’s compliance with U.S. export controls,” Senator Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democratic member on the committee, said in a statement. “The Trump Administration also needs to explain to Congress what ‘input’ was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement.”

ai-fb5a7d58c9.headline: Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it
ai-fb5a7d58c9.fulltext:
When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct. He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” Huang said, according to Wired. “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” still matter. In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO.
It’s an awkward stance for a company whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules. A central part of modern human resources, a code of conduct can seem like a quasi-legal rulebook that lays out unacceptable behavior. But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture. When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for. That’s the risk Huang now faces at Nvidia.
Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct. As Plass sees it, the biggest risk is that employees will become ashamed of their workplace.
“People coming into the workforce now, ethics is incredibly important to them,” he told TechCrunch. “They’re really mindful of the ethical standards of their company. They’re really embarrassed and angry when senior leadership lets them down.”
The consequences of violating the rules aren’t always tangible, but they’re definitely real. Plass gave one example of a company that banned corporate travel to cut costs — only to have its CEO turn up in a VIP box at the Olympics.
“For over a decade afterwards, ‘the Olympics’ was used within that company as an example of the worst thing an employee could do. People would say, ‘Yeah, I shouldn’t have done that, but it’s not like I went to the Olympics.’”
Plass says companies that remove an executive typically do so after an investigation, then try to win back employees. “In most organizations they make a change at the top based on what’s happened,” he said, “and then they will have a hearts-and-minds initiative, to go out to their employee base and their customers and their investors and everybody else, and say, we get it. We’re sorry. We’ve changed. That’s essentially what they do.”
Of course, that playbook is harder to follow at a company like Nvidia, where Huang left without a clear succession plan, and there are serious doubts about whether the company could continue to thrive without him. In cases like that, Plass acknowledges there’s no easy answer.
“I would draw a distinction there between the kind of companies where the CEO is a kind of godhead figure … where the person and the company are almost impossible to separate,” he said. “There it’s much, much harder to deal with.”
In that context, Huang’s stutter-step over the code of conduct is easier to understand. Judging by the employee campaign for his reinstatement, Huang’s return hasn’t created a morale problem so far. But as the coming months put more pressure on Huang and his colleagues, sidestepping the code could end up costing Nvidia something harder to measure — its employees’ pride in the company.

Jensen Huang apologised to Nvidia staff and said he was in therapy on Tuesday, as a stock rally triggered by his shock return as CEO faltered amid persistent doubts over the probes he faces and the fate of the AI investment boom.
“I made some terrible mistakes,” Huang told an hour-long all-hands meeting at the company’s Santa Clara, California, headquarters, The New York Times reported after reviewing a live stream of the event.
He told staff it was “not acceptable” that he had broken a code of conduct he had helped write, and dismissed suggestions that he was back because US President Donald Trump had pressured the board.
But Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had been in contact with directors about Huang’s return. “I spoke to them, let me put it that way,” Trump said. “And I convinced them.”
After vaulting more than 30 per cent on Monday, Nvidia shares were down about 6 per cent at close on Tuesday.
Why does so much of the AI economy hinge on Nvidia’s Jensen Huang?
“The optimism faded quickly” for Nvidia, wrote Fawad Razaqzada of Forex.com, with “questions over corporate governance and board oversight still lingering”.
So far Monday’s surge was a “one day wonder … We are not seeing an upside follow through today at all,” said Ken Mahoney, president and CEO of Mahoney Asset Management.
Huang resigned on November 12 over extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, a departure that sent shares in Nvidia and companies closely linked to the AI buildout tumbling.
Trump was reportedly talked into backing the return of the Taiwan-born CEO after top tech investors told him the US economy and Wall Street depended on it.
Nvidia said on Monday that it had reinstated Huang as chief executive after receiving information from the US government that he did not pose a national security risk.
Trump is also an investor in Nvidia, owning as many as 370,000 shares in the company as of September 30, according to filings.
Shares linked to the AI boom have fallen steeply in recent weeks amid fears that the AI bubble, inflated since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022, was finally bursting.
In downward-trending markets, quick rebounds are common but “tend to get negated and that has been the sequence since early October,” Mahoney said, adding that “sellers have absolute control of the market here”.
Nvidia is central to the AI investment story – its powerful processors are the key tool to train and run the AI models that are believed to be at the heart of a technological revolution.
The massive spending on its AI chips and software, housed in sprawling data centres, catapulted the company into the ranks of the world’s most valuable firms.
Huang used that success to turn Nvidia into a kind of central bank for other AI companies and start-ups, doling out loans and financial guarantees to firms that would otherwise struggle to borrow from traditional lenders.
Investors are also weighing a barrage of legal challenges facing Huang and Nvidia.
The board that let Huang go and then rehired him is still overseeing an internal investigation into concerns that he may have been the target of a Chinese espionage campaign, even though Trump says he has been cleared.
The Justice Department is separately investigating Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that allegedly bought Nvidia processors and routed them to Chinese customers in violation of US export restrictions.
The Securities and Exchange Commission has also reportedly opened a probe into Nvidia’s accounting practices and potentially misleading communication to shareholders.
“Nvidia is a good corporate citizen. That shouldn’t be groundbreaking,” US Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters at an unrelated press conference in Washington on Tuesday.
“If Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation, or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn’t be the message that the president is saying to the American people,” he added.
Huang will nevertheless face lawmakers at a closed-door hearing before three House committees on December 1 and a live-streamed Senate committee hearing on December 3.
Lawmakers from both parties have expressed anger over the circumstances of Huang’s return, and the scrutiny is likely to intensify in January, when Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress.

deep-tech-e2dc72dcad.headline: Jensen Huang is back. The risk to Nvidia and the AI boom remains
deep-tech-e2dc72dcad.fulltext:

Chang Ruay-Shiung is honorary chair professor at the National Taipei University of Business and a former president of the National Taipei University of Business.
Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on November 12, yet on November 23 the board reinstated him. In the intervening days, the company lost around a trillion dollars in market value. When the news of Huang’s reinstatement broke on Monday, Nvidia shares jumped more than 30 per cent and recovered nearly all the losses that followed his exit. Staff crowded the Nvidia headquarters lobby in Santa Clara, California, to welcome him back.
The trouble began on October 29, when The New York Times reported that Washington officials believed a business executive close to Huang worked for Chinese intelligence. On November 8, Huang admitted to his staff that he’d had an extramarital affair. Further reports spoke of relationships with multiple colleagues. Only a few days before Huang’s return, the Nvidia board of directors said it was not considering reinstating him.
Then the mood changed quickly. The board said it had spoken with senior US officials and was sure Huang’s return posed no risk to national security. US President Donald Trump said he spoke with Nvidia’s board, both directly and indirectly. Lawmakers from both major US parties objected to the move, and California Attorney General Rob Bonta said an inquiry into Nvidia’s China dealings would continue.
I see a board that had to choose between a market in free fall and a White House that wanted its champion back. A company this large will always feel the weight of politics. Still, directors who reverse their decisions in just 11 days amid a presidential push will have trouble claiming they run an independent firm.
Nvidia has no named successor and no chief operating officer. Dozens of senior managers report directly to Huang. When he left, nobody could say who would make the hard calls, and the market priced in chaos. His return temporarily ends that chaos, but the move matters well beyond the share price of one company.
Nvidia has built a financing platform of up to US$500 billion with big investment firms to help pay for data centres. Bank of America estimates it also held about US$70 billion in stakes in artificial intelligence (AI) firms as of August, including new cloud rental companies. Analysts feared those deals could slow or cost more without their chief deal maker. Research firm SemiAnalysis said Huang’s personal ties helped win chipmaking capacity in Taiwan and memory supply in Korea. Those ties remain in place.
The week showed how thin the base of the AI boom is. A massively profitable industry spent two weeks unsure whether its biggest supplier could still raise money, book factory time and buy memory chips. All of that rested on one person’s reputation and contacts list.
That is a fragile way to build the base of a new technology. Nvidia extends credit to customers, and those customers then buy Nvidia chips. SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk warns that the sector could run short of cash and that many of the 200 or so small neocloud firms will fail, while Huang says demand will carry them. If the Nvidia leader is wrong, the same single point of trust will be under scrutiny again.
Big buyers are watching, too. Google, Amazon and Microsoft already design their own chips. Any customer who saw their supply hinge on the fortunes of one man will want a second source. Expect the shift to custom chips to accelerate, even as Nvidia keeps its lead.
Export policy is the next test. After the scandal broke, Washington did as many expected and tightened limits on advanced chips reaching China, especially through middlemen. Congress is already talking about new chip security laws. Huang has said that cutting off China is unrealistic and that curbs on chip exports do little. He returns under a security cloud, so he will have little room to say it again.
There is a wider lesson here. The people who run AI firms hold secrets that governments want. Their travel, meetings and private lives are all targets for foreign intelligence. Boards used to treat that as a matter for the legal team. They should now treat it as a board duty. Boards should require clear rules on contact with foreign business partners and honest reports when a rule is violated.
Taiwan’s supply chain barely changed during Huang’s absence. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, Foxconn and Quanta still face strong demand. Huang was born in Taiwan and spent years building trust with Taiwanese firms. Nvidia’s board should ask that this trust be written into contracts, teams and routines. A good relationship should survive the person who started it.
Meanwhile, Huang must deliver on his pledge to Nvidia staff that he will do better the second time round. The easy promise involves himself and his personal life. The harder one involves his company.
Huang should publicly name a successor and hire a chief operating officer. The board should require regular reports from him. Congress and the White House will be watching. Nvidia’s financing platform should stand on assets and contracts, not on one man’s credit.
If he does these things, Nvidia will be stronger than it was before the fall. If he does not, history will repeat itself. When the next crisis happens, the market will teach everyone a much harder lesson.
Chang Ruay-Shiung is honorary chair professor at the National Taipei University of Business and a former president of the National Taipei University of Business. Professor Chang’s research focuses on artificial intelligence, digital transformation, higher education and technology policy. He has published more than 100 academic papers and regularly writes on AI governance and the societal impact of emerging technologies.

Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia’s CEO may steady the chipmaker’s leadership and calm jitters across the global artificial intelligence supply chain, but it is unlikely to ease US export restrictions on China as national security scrutiny in Washington intensifies, analysts say.
The reinstatement of Huang on Monday, ending an 11-day leadership crisis at one of the world’s most valuable companies, sent Nvidia shares surging more than 31 per cent to close at US$165.05 on the Nasdaq, adding nearly US$1 trillion in market value.
At Nvidia’s headquarters in Santa Clara, California, employees greeted his return with cheers and applause, the South China Morning Post reported.
While the move was expected to help restore confidence across the global AI computing supply chain and reinforce prospects for AI infrastructure buildouts, it did not “signal a substantial change in US restrictions on exports of advanced computing chips to China”, Guotai Haitong Securities said in a research note on Tuesday.
A reprieve for Huang, the brokerage noted, did not translate into greater room for Nvidia to sell its products in China. Nvidia confirmed during its earnings call last week that it had halted shipments of US-licensed Hopper chips, including the H200, to the country.
Analysts warned against interpreting the leadership reversal as a softening of Washington’s tech containment strategy.
“Congressional momentum towards tighter restrictions is still moving ahead,” said Lizzi C. Lee, a fellow on the Chinese economy at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s (ASPI) Centre for China Analysis.
Dan Ives, an analyst at US merchant bank Yorkville Ives, echoed that assessment in a note to clients on Monday, writing that Huang’s return had done little to clear the regulatory cloud hanging over the company.
Both Nvidia’s internal investigation and government inquiries remained active, he said, while “the export question has not been resolved”.
The dramatic turnaround caps a tumultuous period that began on November 12, when Huang resigned after admitting to marital infidelity, following reports linking him to Alice Huang, a businesswoman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence. Beijing has repeatedly dismissed the espionage allegation.
His departure sparked a lobbying campaign by employees, investors and Silicon Valley figures, including Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, calling for his return. Although Huang signalled his willingness to come back at the height of the push, Nvidia’s board initially resisted before reversing course on Monday.
In a statement, the board said it voted unanimously to reinstate Huang following input from US government officials, concluding that his return “poses no national security risk”.
Nvidia also said days earlier that it had established a national security and export control committee, made up entirely of independent directors, to oversee trade-compliance matters.
Behind the scenes, US President Donald Trump played a decisive role, reportedly dialling into an Nvidia board meeting to advocate for Huang’s return, according to US news outlet Semafor. Trump later told American broadcaster CNBC he had spoken with board members directly and indirectly to convince them to reverse course.
ASPI’s Lee said the White House’s intervention “mattered enormously” and underscored how central Nvidia and its founder had become to Washington’s AI ambitions, though she cautioned that the episode could invite even closer scrutiny of Nvidia’s ties to the Trump administration.
Resistance on Capitol Hill showed no signs of fading. Republican leaders of three key House panels, including the House Select Committee on China, confirmed that Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter remained scheduled to appear for congressional interviews in early December.
“The Nvidia board’s brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed,” the lawmakers said in a joint statement on Monday.
They reiterated their commitment to investigating the alleged smuggling of Nvidia chips and their role in advancing China’s AI capabilities.
Beyond direct sales to China, the fallout threatened to complicate the broader global AI buildout, according to investment research firm Morningstar. While Huang’s return was likely to reduce the risk of disruptions to Nvidia’s product road map, Morningstar warned that a return to business as usual was far from assured.
Last week, the US Bureau of Industry and Security issued new rules requiring licences for advanced chips sent to overseas data centres that remotely supply large-scale computing power to Chinese and other restricted entities, closing what Washington viewed as a major loophole.
“We don’t believe that Nvidia is back to even with the start of the saga,” Morningstar said. “The company will face restrictions in selling leading artificial intelligence gear to countries, mostly in Southeast Asia, that were renting cloud workloads to Chinese AI model builders.”

The public reaction to Jensen Huang’s return has been mixed at best, raising the hackles of lawmakers and corporate governance experts. Even the stock price took a bit of a dip after surging by over 30% on Monday. Within the company, however, the mood appears to be considerably lighter.
In videos that are circulating across social media, Huang received a hero’s welcome at Nvidia headquarters, where his employees lined the walls cheering for him. Between chants of “Jensen! Jensen!” and “We love you, Jensen,” he addressed his staff in a display of contrition.
“I’m terribly sorry for putting all of you through all of this,” he said. “I’ve made some very terrible mistakes, and I’m going to work on coming back.” After an employee threw her arms around Huang in a tight hug—lasting over 10 seconds—he continued: “Thank you all for the second chance. I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around.”
Many Nvidia employees have taken to LinkedIn to express their relief over Huang’s return, seemingly overlooking the indiscretions that led to his ousting. They heaped praise on their newly reinstated CEO, describing him as the “heartbeat of Nvidia” and “one of a kind.”
One employee even invoked Charles Dickens, paraphrasing the opening of A Tale of Two Cities: “It was the worst of times, it is the best of times. It was the season of Darkness, it is the season of Light. It was the winter of despair, it is the spring of hope. We had nothing before us, we have everything before us.”
Another employee claimed he always knew Huang would return to Nvidia: “When Jensen stepped down, many said their goodbyes and thanked him for his legacy. I stayed quiet—not out of indifference, but because deep down I knew there is only one boss, and he would be back.”
A former robotics engineer at Nvidia—who quit rather publicly after Huang’s resignation—congratulated him on X and admitted he made a hasty decision. “Looking back, I may have moved too quickly, and I don’t want to rush into another major decision. For now, I’d like to take some time to rest, reflect, and think carefully about my future. As part of that, I’m open to exploring the possibility of returning.”

climate-energy-1b3f011ce6.headline: India Proposes Battery Storage For Rooftop Solar Above 10 kW
climate-energy-1b3f011ce6.fulltext:

India Proposes Battery Storage For Rooftop Solar Above 10 kW
A draft amendment to the Electricity (Rights of Consumers) Rules proposes a default storage requirement for rooftop solar systems above 10 kW
Key Takeaways
- According to a MoP proposal, battery storage could be required for rooftop solar systems above 10 kW
- The proposed requirement is at least 20% of the system's daily energy generation, unless a different proportion is specified
- The storage provision is expected to take effect from April 1, 2028, under the draft
India's Ministry of Power (MoP) has proposed requiring battery energy storage systems (BESS) for rooftop solar installations above 10 kW, with effect from April 1, 2028.
The proposal is part of the draft Electricity (Rights of Consumers) Amendment Rules, 2026. It proposes that the storage provision will take effect where State Electricity Regulatory Commissions (SERCs) have not specified a different capacity threshold.
The proposal gives state regulators flexibility to determine the threshold and storage requirements based on local conditions.
As per the draft, SERC may prescribe the capacity threshold above which prosumers must install energy storage. The required storage capacity would be at least 20% of the renewable energy system's total daily generation, unless the respective Commission specifies a different proportion.
In the absence of a threshold set by a State Commission, the proposed requirement would apply to renewable energy systems with an installed capacity exceeding 10 kW.
The ministry said falling battery storage costs, supported by economies of scale, technological innovation and market competition, have improved the economic viability of storage deployment.
Integrating batteries with rooftop solar could also help shift surplus electricity to evening hours, support grid stability and ease operational pressure on distribution companies.
Additionally, the draft also proposes allowing consumers, including commercial and industrial (C&I) units and MSMEs, to install rooftop solar capacity beyond their sanctioned load. This will be subject to limits set by State Commissions based on local grid capacity and technical requirements.
However, consumers would be allowed to feed electricity into the grid only up to their sanctioned load, unless the distribution company approves a higher limit. Power injected beyond the approved limit would not qualify for compensation and could attract penalties.
The draft also proposes delaying the rollout of Time-of-Day (ToD) tariffs to align it with smart meter installation. Under the proposal, ToD tariffs would apply to consumers with a load of 10 kW and above from April 1, 2028, and to other non-agricultural consumers from April 1, 2029.
This will give state regulators the flexibility to decide solar and peak hours based on electricity demand and generation patterns in their respective states, instead of following fixed timings.
Earlier, the Central Electricity Authority (CEA) proposed making co-located energy storage mandatory for new ground-mounted solar and onshore wind projects commissioned after July 1, 2027 (see India May Mandate Storage For Solar, Wind Projects From 2027).

Elon Musk, the world’s richest person, has pledged to give every child in the US two shares in SpaceX, the space and AI company he runs, worth a total of almost $18bn.
In a brief post on X, the social media platform that he owns, Musk said children will receive one share from the company itself, and one from him personally. SpaceX announced earlier on Wednesday that it would contribute one newly issued share of its Class A common stock ‌to every currently active Trump Account, and that ‌Musk will match the number of shares it donates.
The Trump account program was designed to give every American under 18 a stake in the stock market, to help build wealth from an early age. In a separate post, Musk said the company shares will be transferred next month, with his own to follow later. “The share directly from me will be transferred when my lockup expires in June next year,” he wrote.
In October, Musk, whose net worth is around $824bn, announced his intention to give one of his SpaceX shares to every child in America. “This will be the first of many,” he said in a post on X at the time. As of June, he held about 6.42bn shares in the company.
Most of Musk’s philanthropic efforts have been conducted via the Musk Foundation, which reportedly holds around $16bn in assets.
In October, SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell and her husband pledged a share of their SpaceX stock to each of more than 2 million children under the Trump account initiative.
Musk and rival AI company Anthropic have recently detailed their sharply different approaches for sharing the spoils of the AI boom. Other major, long-running philanthropy ventures include those of Berkshire Hathaway chair emeritus Warren Buffett, who is reported to have given away $60bn, with the intention of doing the same with most of the rest of his $150bn fortune.

Spain’s Pablo Hernandez de Cos will be the next head of the European Central Bank, taking over from Christine Lagarde, diplomats said on Thursday.
His nomination comes at a time of tension on European bond markets and before a series of high-stakes elections in Europe next year, including in France.
Hernandez de Cos, 55, has been head of the Swiss-based Bank for International Settlements (BIS) since last year, and previously led the Bank of Spain from 2018 to 2024.
The ECB is the central bank for the 21 countries that use the euro, setting interest rates that influence borrowing costs across the economy, from mortgages to credit-card repayments.
“The Netherlands will support the consensus for the three nominations for the ECB board,” an EU diplomat said.
That diplomat and a second confirmed it meant Hernandez de Cos won the support of euro area countries over Klaas Knot, former head of the Dutch central bank.
In addition to the ECB top job, France’s Laurence Boone and Germany’s Markus Brunnermeier were the sole candidates to fill two vacant seats on the bank’s executive board.
Thanks to a grand bargain on the package between France and Germany, Hernandez de Cos was chosen in a decision that came after EU leaders’ talks in Brussels.
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten on Thursday informed European Council chief Antonio Costa “that the Netherlands values a consensual decision on the ECB presidency. An important signal to financial markets”, a diplomat said.
The Frankfurt-based institution has said Lagarde would step down in February 2027, several months before her term expires in October next year.
Lagarde was given a warm welcome during the summit, with leaders lavishing praise on her tenure, an official said.
Thursday’s green light triggers a formal process during which European leaders will later in the day approve the candidates for each ECB post.
The bank’s governing council and European Parliament will then formally back the nominations.
Spain’s Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who is battling unfavourable polling before a general election on Sunday, hailed the choice on social media, saying it reflects “a Spain that leads in Europe”.
He pointed to the Spanish chief of the European Investment Bank, Nadia Calvino, and the EU executive’s second most senior official, Teresa Ribera, as other figures of influence.
Known as a consensus builder, Hernandez de Cos is a career central banker whose pragmatic approach has earned him respect.

Ukraine says Russia hits two grain ships carrying 100,000 tonnes near Odesa
Russia attacked two foreign grain ships near Odesa, Ukraine said, as grain exports from the country's Black Sea ports remain disrupted by security risks and soaring insurance costs.
Russia attacked two foreign cargo ships carrying more than 100,000 metric tons of grain overnight near Ukraine's Black Sea port of Odesa, Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergiy Koretskyi said on Thursday.
Koretskyi did not say where the grain originated nor where the vessels had loaded their cargo.
Ukraine has said grain shipments from its key Black Sea ports around Odesa have all but stopped since late July after Russia sharply intensified attacks on grain terminals and merchant vessels.
Russia says it does not attack civilian targets.
Before the escalation, the three ports in the Odesa hub handled about 90% of Ukraine's agricultural and metallurgical exports.
Kyiv has not formally banned port operations, but shipowners have avoided the ports because of security risks, while soaring insurance costs have deterred traders.
President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said earlier this year that shipments from Odesa ports were taking place only intermittently, while Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskiy has said no exports were moving through them.
Analysts' data show that Ukraine's state railway continues to transport grain towards Black Sea ports.
Consultancy APK-Inform reported this week that 429 grain wagons were dispatched towards Odesa between November 12 and November 18, four times the level recorded a week earlier.
Ukraine does not publish official data on shipments from its Black Sea ports, saying agricultural exports have instead been redirected to Danube River ports or moved by rail across land borders with eastern European countries.
Official data showed Ukraine had exported 7.6 million tons of grain so far in the 2026/27 July-June season, down from 11.5 million tons in the same period a year earlier.

The fertiliser crisis triggered by the Gulf war has exposed a strategic vulnerability in Indian agriculture: the country’s ability to sustain food production remains partly dependent on industrial facilities, energy supplies and shipping routes beyond its borders.The disruption of fertiliser supply chains across West Asia has reinforced the urgency of expanding domestic production capacity and insulating Indian farmers from geopolitical shocks.The government’s November 25 approval of six gas-based urea manufacturing projects, involving an estimated investment of ₹54,000 crore, represents a significant intervention in this direction. Together, the projects will add 76.2 lakh tonnes to India’s annual urea manufacturing capacity, potentially reducing import dependence, strengthening fertiliser availability and improving the resilience of agricultural supply chains.The projects, approved under the National Investment Policy for Urea (NIPU)-2026, cover six locations: Chennai, Nangal, Shahjahanpur, Panagarh, Gadepan and Jagdishpur. With participation from public sector enterprises, cooperatives and private manufacturers, the programme combines industrial expansion with the technological modernisation of ageing fertiliser manufacturing infrastructure. Each project will have an annual installed capacity of 12.7 lakh tonnes.The scale of India's import vulnerability is evident from the mismatch between domestic production and consumption. According to the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, India consumes approximately 400 lakh tonnes of urea annually, against domestic production of 293.30 lakh tonnes in 2025–26. Although production has expanded considerably from 225 lakh tonnes in 2014–15, rising agricultural demand has constrained progress towards self-sufficiency.The Gulf war aggravated this structural vulnerability. West Asia is a major centre of global fertiliser manufacturing, benefiting from abundant natural gas reserves and relatively low production costs. Disruptions to maritime trade, energy supplies and manufacturing operations in the region have complicated fertiliser procurement. For India, the consequences extend beyond the availability of imported urea. Higher international fertiliser and natural gas prices also translate into greater subsidy expenditure for the government.The procurement of fertilisers during periods of geopolitical instability is particularly challenging because agricultural demand is seasonal. Delays in shipments during critical sowing periods can affect crop productivity and rural incomes. Domestic manufacturing provides greater control over production schedules, inventories and distribution, although it cannot entirely eliminate exposure to international energy markets.The government's investment strategy builds on the experience of the New Investment Policy of 2012, which facilitated the establishment of six manufacturing units, including facilities at Ramagundam, Gorakhpur, Sindri and Barauni. The new policy seeks to improve the commercial viability of fertiliser manufacturing by providing a return-on-equity band of 12–16%, alongside mechanisms to mitigate foreign exchange risks and improve transparency in production costs.An important dimension of the latest approvals is the replacement of technologically obsolete manufacturing infrastructure. The Madras Fertilizers facility in Chennai is over six decades old, while National Fertilizers Limited's Nangal facility has been operating for more than five decades. Replacing energy-intensive plants with modern facilities could lower natural gas consumption per tonne of urea, improve operational safety and reduce manufacturing costs.However, the combined installed capacity of 76.2 lakh tonnes should not be interpreted as an equivalent net addition to domestic production, since some projects will replace existing facilities. The actual reduction in import dependence will depend on commissioning schedules, capacity utilisation, retirement of older plants and future consumption patterns.There is also a fundamental limitation to India's strategy of achieving fertiliser self-sufficiency through gas-based manufacturing. Natural gas is both a feedstock and an energy source for urea production. With India dependent on imported liquefied natural gas to meet a significant portion of its requirements, expanding domestic urea production could partially shift import dependence from finished fertilisers to energy feedstocks.Diversification of natural gas procurement, expansion of domestic gas production and improvements in manufacturing efficiency must therefore accompany the capacity expansion programme. Over the longer term, advances in green ammonia production using renewable hydrogen could provide an alternative pathway, subject to improvements in commercial viability.The supply-side intervention must also be accompanied by reforms in fertiliser consumption. India’s heavily subsidised urea pricing regime has encouraged excessive nitrogen application and discouraged balanced use of phosphorus, potassium and other nutrients. Indiscriminate urea consumption contributes to soil degradation, groundwater contamination, declining nutrient-use efficiency and greenhouse gas emissions.The policy challenge is to reduce excessive consumption without imposing additional financial burdens on farmers. Soil testing, precision agriculture, crop-specific nutrient recommendations and gradual rationalisation of fertiliser subsidies could help achieve this objective. Improvements in nutrient-use efficiency would reduce import requirements and subsidy expenditure without compromising agricultural productivity.The ₹54,000 crore investment programme is, therefore, as much an exercise in economic and strategic security as in agricultural policy. It offers an opportunity to modernise India's fertiliser industry, reduce exposure to volatile international markets and strengthen the foundations of food security.Its ultimate success, however, cannot be measured exclusively in tonnes of additional urea produced. India must simultaneously reduce the energy intensity of manufacturing, diversify feedstock supplies and correct distortions in fertiliser consumption. Genuine fertiliser security requires not only the capacity to produce more urea but also the ability to achieve higher agricultural productivity with less of it.
